item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Carl Mays
item.author: Andrew Mearns
item.content:encoded: Carl Mays probably would’ve enjoyed one single entry in the annals of baseball lore that doesn’t mention the most regrettable of the thousands of pitches that he threw across a 15-year career that saw him capture four World Series titles. Alas, even on his 135th birthday, we cannot grant that wish. No matter how great he was on the mound, his story will always be tied to that of Cleveland shortstop Ray Chapman. That’s just how it is. November 12, 1891 (Liberty, KY) April 4, 1971 (El Cajon, CA): 1919-23Mays was born in Kentucky to a Methodist minister named William Mays (ah, baseball coincidences), who died when Carl was just 12 years old. The family had moved to Missouri by then, but they packed up again after William’s death, en route to Kingfisher, Oklahoma. It was a sad time for Mays’ family, but he did get the opportunity to meet his cousin, John Long. He was a catcher, and he introduced Mays to the game. Pitching to Long, Mays developed the raw skills to attract the notice of traveling teams.At the age of 20, Mays signed with the Class D Western Tri-State League’s Boise Irrigators, who offered him $90 per month. Mays was certainly worth the deal, as he pitched to a 2.08 ERA, 0.930 WHIP, and a 22-9 record in 280.2 innings. He moved up to the Class B team in Portland and again had a fine season, though won/loss record (10-15) deceived his true performance (2.45 ERA, 1.024 WHIP in 250 innings), and it was enough to get a new contract for 1914 with the Providence Grays, a Rhode Island team owned by the Detroit Tigers.The Boston Red Sox purchased the Grays from the Tigers during the season, and Mays attracted Boston’s interested with a fantastic season: 24-8 and a 2.57 ERA in 273.1 innings. Another young pitcher joined him down the stretch named Babe Ruth, and their pitching helped Providence win the pennant. By the beginning of next season, Mays was a major-league pitcher.The submariner worked mostly out of the bullpen in his rookie season, appearing in 38 games but 131.2 innings overall of 90 ERA- and 69 FIP- ball. He threw hard and was not at all afraid to throw high and inside to back hitters off the plate. Even as a rookie, he made an enemy of Ty Cobb, whose own nasty attitude clashed with Mays. On one occasion, Cobb was knocked down and then dragged a bunt up the first base line, where he spiked Mays with his sharp cleats and cut his leg. Boston and Detroit fought hard for the pennant in 1915; a 100-win season was not good enough to win the title for Detroit. Boston beat the Phillies in five games for the 1915 World Series title, but while he was a champion in his first season, Mays did not appear in any of the games.The next couple seasons saw Mays slowly transition from splitting time more evenly between the ‘pen and rotation to becoming an established rotation presence and the ace of a championship staff. Although he was a bit of a loner, there was no denying his competitiveness on the mound. The Red Sox repeated as champions in 1916, and Mays had his best year in Boston in 1917, pitching to a 1.74 ERA (69 ERA-) in 289 innings while also unsurprisingly leading the league in hit by pitches. Only two pitchers in baseball had a better ERA than Mays that year and despite the HBPs, he had a 1.052 WHIP. His pitches simply sank, and many batters could not do any better than hitting it on the ground while hoping it found a hole in the infield:Yankees infielder Roger Peckinpaugh said Mays threw “a very ‘heavy’ ball. It sinks and when you catch it, it feels heavy enough to almost go through your glove.” Horace Ford, who batted against Mays in the National League, said that hitting Mays’s fastball “was like hitting a chuck of lead. It would go clunk and you’d beat it into the ground.”– Allan Wood, SABRBoston finished nine games behind the White Sox for the AL pennant that year, but another fine season by Mays in 1918 brought them back on top. While his ERA and ERA- jumped a bit to 2.21 and 84, respectively, his WHIP was almost identical and he led the league in both shutouts (8) and complete games (30). Those marks were made more impressive by the fact that the season ended early after 126 games on September 2nd due to World War I. The Red Sox played the Cubs in the Fall Classic, and Mays received the ball in Game 3 with the series tied at one game apiece. He beat the Cubs 2-1, going the distance with just one walk allowed, scattering seven hits. Boston and Chicago split the next two games, so Mays got the start in Game 6 to close out the Cubbies, and he did just that by spinning a three-hitter in another 2-1 victory. Mays was the last man to throw a pitch for a championship Red Sox team in the next 86 years.Although his teammates were not fond of Mays for his somewhat antisocial personality and irritance on the mound when they committed errors, it seemed as though Boston and Mays had a fine relationship. It all came to a sudden halt in 1919. Boston struggled to give him much run support, and Mays became highly frustrated with the offense. From a personal standpoint, his Missouri home had burned down, and he grew so annoyed with the Philadelphia fans during one series that he hurled a baseball from the dugout at a fan. Finally, in a July 13th game against the White Sox, catcher Wally Schang clocked him in the head with a throw on a stolen base by Eddie Collins.Soon afterward, manager and future Yankees GM Ed Barrow removed him from the game, and he stormed off the field, chucking the ball against the backstop. Mays was suspended by the Red Sox and told sportswriters that he demanded a trade. Soon, owner Harry Frazee obliged, sending Mays to the Yankees on July 29th in exchange for two unremarkable pitchers and $40,000.“Carl, this is [co-owner] Cap Huston of the Yankees. I called to find out if you would be interested in pitching for the Yankees. If you are, there’s a good chance of my swinging a deal for you tonight, but I didn’t want to get all tangled up in negotiations if you wouldn’t pitch for us.”“Well, how about the money?”“We’ll have no problems there. Just pack your bag, and by the time you get here, we’ll be ready to talk contract.”– excerpted from Marty Appel’s “Pinstripe Empire”AL president Ban Johnson was furious about the trade since a suspended player was dealt and essentially controlled his own fate over the authority of the Red Sox owner. The reserve clause was supposed to bind a player to his team without much control over it, but Mays worked around the system. He demanded that the trade be voided and that Mays be returned to Boston, but Yankee owners Jacob Ruppert and Cap Huston flat-out refused and told Johnson that if necessary, they would go to court to keep Mays on the Yankees. New York State Supreme Court Justice Robert F. Wagner granted a temporary injunction allowing Mays to pitch for the Yankees.Johnson’s decision was rendered meaningless, and Mays made 13 starts for the Yankees down the stretch as the team bid to pass the infamous “Black Sox” in the AL pennant race. Although the White Sox ended up running away with the pennant as the Yankees finished in third place with an 80-59 record, it was not Mays’ fault by any means. He was outstanding, pitching to a 1.65 ERA and 51 ERA-, winning nine of his starts, completing all but one of them, and throwing a shutout as well. In just 13 starts, he was worth 2.6 rWAR and 2.2 fWAR for a rising Yankees team. They had their ace, and now they needed a hitting star. They enlisted Mays’ former rotationmate Ruth, who was a pretty fair hitter.With Mays and Ruth in tow, the Yankees had a superb team ready for the 1920 campaign. They finished the year with a then-franchise record 95 wins and a .617 winning percentage, though they ended up behind pennant-winning Cleveland by two games. The race between the two teams was sadly marred by tragedy in a game on August 16th at the Yankees’ home, the Polo Grounds.Mays was in the midst of another fine season, wherein he led the league with six shutouts, pitched 312 innings, and ended with a 3.06 ERA (81 ERA-). The unpopular Mays faced perhaps his polar opposite at the plate leading off the fifth inning in beloved Cleveland shortstop Ray Chapman, a perennially fantastic player who had already amassed a 28.9 fWAR career in just nine years and 1,051 games with Cleveland. He was only 29, a potential Hall of Famer in the making. Even Cobb liked him. However, Chapman had a tendency to lean over the plate, and Mays threw an inside fastball toward him to start this at-bat. What happened next was unclear: either Chapman ducked unfortunately right into the ball’s path attempting a drag bunt, or he never moved at all. Either way, it got him square in the temple with a sickeningly loud crack.It struck Chapman so hard that the ball caromed back toward the mound, and Mays’ immediate action was to throw the ball to first base in case it hit Chapman’s bat. Chapman’s teammates helped him off the field, as he was still conscious. They brought him to St. Lawrence Hospital, where he was diagnosed with a fractured skull and died the next day, the only player to ever die as the result of a pitch in an MLB game.“It was the most regrettable incident of my career, and I would give anything if I could undo what has happened.“– Carl MaysThe whole incident was a horrible experience for everyone involved; Mays was contrite but overall did not handle it particularly well, noting that there was scuff on the ball (which he always normally liked to do anyway), and that he didn’t expect Chapman to duck into the ball. He insisted to his dying day that he did not throw at Chapman. Regardless, the tragedy only emphasized the reason why baseball banned the spitball at the beginning of the year, with only those who already threw it allowed to use it via grandfather clause. Strangely, it still took over 35 years before players started wearing helmets in the batter’s box.Mays became synonymous with Chapman’s death, and while he pitched another nine years in The Show, most people only remember Mays for that tragic pitch. Mays’ best season in New York actually occurred the very next year. He did what he could to put the incident behind him and paced the league with 27 wins, 49 games (38 starts), and a career-high 336.2 innings pitched. He was brilliant in a 4.5-fWAR campaign, and the Bombers outlasted Cleveland to win their first pennant in franchise history. Mays completed nine of his ten starts down the stretch and even tossed in a relief appearance; the Yankees won all but one of those games.In the first game of the unusual best-of-nine, all-Polo Grounds World Series against John McGraw’s Giants, Mays put the Yankees ahead with a dominant five-hit shutout. He didn’t walk anyone, and only two batters made it past first base. The teams split the next two games, and Mays had the chance to give the Yankees a 3-1 series lead in Game 4, but Phil Douglas outpitched him. Mays held a slim 1-0 lead into the top of the eighth, but an Irish Meusel triple, singles by Johnny Rawlings and Fred Snyder, and a two-run double by George Burns gave the Giants three runs. The Yankees lost 4-2 to even the series.Manager Miller Huggins turned back to Mays on just two days’ rest in Game 7 with the series even at 3-3. The only other starter in the pitching well was Waite Hoyt, so the Yankees were desperate. Mays did just about all he could do, allowing just six hits to the Giants, but a two-out double by Snyder in the seventh scored Rawlings, who reached on an error by second baseman Aaron Ward. Again, the Yankees were unable to do much against Douglas, and they lost 2-1. The Giants finished off the series five games to three on the strength of a 1-0 four-hit shutout by Art Nehf against Hoyt. There was some talk that Mays fixed the game in the two losses, but that was never proven and seems highly risky and unlikely given the then-recent lifetime bans suffered by the “Black Sox” players who threw the 1919 World Series. The Giants were just a damn good team, and they beat one of the best pitchers in baseball during the tiring late innings of two games.With almost 2,000 regular season and playoff innings on Mays’ arm in seven seasons, he began to decline somewhat at age 30 in 1922. He was still a solid pitcher with a 3.60 ERA and a 90 ERA-, but he was never as dominant as he was in ‘21 ever again. The Yankees won their second straight pennant in ’22 and again faced McGraw’s Giants in the World Series. This time, it was not nearly as close. The series returned to a best-of-seven and the Giants won Games 1 and 3 to take a 2-0 lead (Game 2 ended in a 3-3 tie called on account of darkness). Mays got the nod in Game 4, but despite getting staked to an early two-run advantage, a four-run fifth led to a 4-3 loss. The Giants finished off their undefeated series with a 5-3 victory in Game 5, as Nehf finished off the Yankees for the second straight year.The Yankees had grown weary of Mays by 1923, and they reportedly sought to trade him before the season. Nothing happened though, so Huggins just barely used him throughout the Yankees’ pennant three-peat. Mays pitched poorly when he did appear, so it was not as though the Yankees were squandering anyone valuable. He did not appear in the Fall Classic of the Yankees’ first championship, as they finally beat the Giants.The Cincinnati Reds bought Mays from the Yankees after the ’23 campaign, and he managed to stick around with them for five more years, alternating between healthy and injury-plagued seasons. He had a comeback season at age 34 in ’26, leading the NL with 24 complete games and pitching to a 3.14 ERA (85 ERA-) in 281 innings, a 4.7 fWAR season. The Reds finished just two games behind the Cardinals for the NL pennant. Exhausted, Mays pitched just 144.2 innings over his next two years with the Reds, and finished his MLB career with one mediocre season on McGraw’s Giants as the decade came to a close.Mays pitched two years in the minor league American Association and Pacific Coast League, then officially ended his playing career at age 40. His baseball career did not fully conclude though; he had made amends with the Cleveland organization and scouted for them, Milwaukee, and Kansas City over the next 20 years. He lived until he was 79 years old, passing away in ‘71 with the game a whole lot different than it was when he began. Mays was a crucial member of the first Yankee teams of any sustained success, and his contributions to those teams should not be forgotten.See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: Netcompany Ineos end long-term partnership with Continental to switch to Pirelli tyres for 2027
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: Netcompany Ineos will race on Pirelli tyres from 2027 onwards, bringing an end to a a long-term partnership with Continental. Launching as Sky Procycling in 2010, the British team used a range of tyres from manufacturers like Veloflex, FMB, and Vittoria in their early years, but have consistently used Continental for more than a decade now.However, a new three-year agreement with Pirelli was. announced on Thursday. "Pirelli bring a huge amount of technical expertise and a real commitment to innovation, so it's exciting to have them working closely with our riders and performance team," said the team's Director of Racing, Geraint Thomas."It's not just about the equipment we race on, but how we can work together to keep developing, so we're really looking forward to building that relationship and seeing what we can achieve together."Netcompany Ineos will make their racing debut on Pirelli rubber at the Santos Tour Down Under in January. 'Marginal gains' is still a phrase that's closely linked to Netcompany Ineos, and there is some mention of that philosophy in the Pirelli press release. Pirelli says the partnership will focus on developing 'technical solutions' to the demands of WorldTour cycling. There's also a mention of 'technical assessment' being a key step in the development of the partnership. In simple language, this could point to the team testing the Pirelli tyres against the Continental GP 5000 S TR and TT TR tyres they have been racing on until now. Pirelli already supplies two WorldTour teams: Lidl-Trek and Alpecin-Premier Tech.It sounds like Netcompany Ineos will primarily use the Pirelli P Zero Race SL-R tyre as well as the P Zero Race RS model. The team also switched wheels at the start of this year, moving from Shimano Dura-Ace wheels to Scope models. Perhaps the Scope wheels and Pirelli tyre combination has proven to be faster. We tested road tyres in our CN Labs tyre test in 2024, testing both Continental and Pirelli models, but that test didn't include the then unreleased P Zero Race SL-R.Pirelli launched its flagship P Zero Race SL-R tyre in March this year. The tyres use PAAS (Pirelli Advanced Aerodynamic System technology), which adds material to the sidewalls of the slick tyre to improve aerodynamic performance when mounted to a rim. Pirelli claimed rolling resistance and aero performance had improved considerably compared to its P Zero RACE RS model. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Subscribe for unlimited access to our comprehensive news coverage, industry-leading CN Labs testing, expert columnists, and so much more. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

item.title: Factor Bikes strengthens its partnership with Team Amani with three-year title sponsorship deal
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: After recently announcing that it will support Bahrain Victorious for 2027 and beyond, Factor Bikes is extending its presence in the pro peloton by becoming a title sponsor for Team Amani.The team will be known as Team Amani Factor Racing from 2027 until the end of 2029, with Factor’s founder, Rob Gitelis, convinced the team can reach the highest levels of the women’s sport.Factor and Amani have worked together for four years, but the new deal will not only include the bike brand in the team’s name, but also bring the team into Factor's performance programme, as they do with their other pro teams. As such, they will ride the company’s Ostro VAM and Ostro Gravel frames rolling on Black Inc wheels. The partnership will include not only the Women’s Continental road team, but also their off-road programme and the Black Mamba Development squad.Amani is a proudly African team, competing with a roster comprised entirely of women from the continent. While they’ve been around as a club-level team for a few years, they graduated to UCI level only at the start of the 2026 season. During that time, they took three wins, all at fourth-tier .2 level races in Africa, though they showed real promise on European roads, especially at the Volta Ciclista Catalunya, where Haftu Eyerusalem Reda finished 20th in the general classification in the mountainous three-day race.Despite their status as one of the youngest teams in the bunch, Amani have stated their ambition to ride the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift in 2028. However, with UCI Regulations as they currently are, achieving that is likely to require the team to shift up a level from Women’s Continental to ProTeam to guarantee a start at the biggest race on the calendar."Of everything we’re doing in racing, Amani is the project I feel most personally invested in," Gitelis said. "We’re back in the men’s WorldTour and expanding our racing programme, which is exciting, but I want to devote real time and resources to this over the next three years. I believe this team can compete at the sharp end of the women’s WorldTour with the right support, experience and time. "Beyond racing, I believe the opportunities that it creates can change the lives of the women involved. That’s why Amani belongs within Factor Racing."Mikel Delagrange, Amani’s founder, welcomed Factor’s extended commitment, saying: "What has impressed me most about Factor is that when they say they’re going to do something, they do it. Every commitment they’ve made to this team over the past four years has been planned carefully and delivered in full."That’s rare in this world, and it’s exactly what a team like ours needs. Taking on title sponsorship is the biggest step yet, and I trust it completely because I’ve seen how Factor works. We have a clear goal for 2028, and the right partner to help us get there."

item.title: Tsolov gets twin F1 2027 reserve role to prepare him for race seat
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Red Bull has named Nikola Tsolov the official reserve driver of both of its Formula 1 teams in 2027 with a programme “designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level”.Tsolov missed out on a 2027 Racing Bulls seat as Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad were both handed extensions into next year. But Red Bull has made clear Tsolov is still very much the next driver in line for an F1 seat, confirming on the same day Lawson and Lindblad were confirmed for 2027 that Tsolov would be made reserve. Tsolov is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title with 2027 Haas F1 driver Rafael Camara and Alex Dunne, having taken six race wins with two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi remaining. Tsolov finished runner-up to Camara in his third Formula 3 campaign last year. Red Bull's announcement read: “In his new role, Nikola will undertake an extensive development programme, combining simulator and development work with valuable track experience through Free Practice sessions, Testing of Previous Cars (TPC), selected test sessions and tyre testing. “Alongside his responsibilities as a reserve driver, the programme is designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level.” Tsolov said he was “incredibly happy and grateful” to Red Bull for the opportunity. “My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver,” he said.“Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting. I’m confident that with the team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.” Tsolov impressed Racing Bulls with his FP1 debut in Mexico where he compared favourably to 2026 rookie Lindblad. “Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years,” Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies said.“To fight for the championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. “What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. “This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.”

item.title: Tsolov lands reserve driver role for F1 2027
PHD chemistry and three types of sand – Inside the CeramicSpeed chain lubricant test labs
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: Cyclists have been applying lubricants to their bicycle chains for well over a century. From the invention of 3-in-1 oil in 1894 to condition-specific wet and dry formulations, through to hot waxing and the performance-focused, watt-saving lubricants we have today. There are now countless products promising an increase in speed, quietness and longevity. Currently, no industry-standard test procedures exist for chain lubricants and waxes, and what is the best thing to test? There are established big names, but how can you tell an effective product from one that might actually do your drivetrain harm?CeramicSpeed is one brand that formulates and tests all of its own chain waxes and lubricants in-house. A fact which possibly draws less attention than the brand's more visible high-end ceramic bearings and OSPW pulley wheel systems. I visited the CeramicSpeed headquarters in Holstebro, Denmark, where the brand has dedicated chain-lubricant formulation and test labs in an attempt to answer a few of the questions the chain lube nerd in me had, and to learn more about how you go about formulating an effective chain lubricant or wax, testing it and bringing it to market.The origins of the modern-day chain waxing revolution lie with Jason Smith’s Friction Facts chain lubricant and testing business, which carried out some of the very first, if not the first, dedicated drivetrain friction testing over a decade ago. CeramicSpeed acquired FrictionFacts in 2016, including at least one of its test machines, and then built on Smith’s original UFO product foundation. Smith joined the business as well, and later worked on the Driven chainless drivetrain project, but is no longer involved.Product development and rigorous testing are a cornerstone of the CeramicSpeed product philosophy. The brand commits plenty of time to formulating and testing chain products. Various brands carry out their own lubricant testing; some do none. It varies, and more than one brand markets its products as the fastest. ZeroFriction, an Australian independent testing company, is a reference point for many who are interested in lubricants and testing, but a lot happens behind closed doors.CeramicSpeed chain products begin life in the brand's lab. Glass flasks line a wall, and at the end of a workbench topped with several machines that look a bit like microscopes, there’s a cabinet full of the base ingredients used to produce chain lubes and wax. This being Denmark early in the year, the carpet of snow on the ground outside matches the colour of the product in some of the bottles today. Lina Søbjerg Madsen, a PHD chemist, and Michael Pedersen, Development Engineer, have both been with CeramicSpeed for the best part of a decade and form the backbone of the brand's wax and lubricant development and testing programme. If you have used a CeramicSpeed lube or wax product in that time, they will have developed and tested it.CeramicSpeed wax and lube products are both wax-based. Hot melt wax is a blend of pure waxes, including what Søbjerg Madsen tells me, with a grin, is her 'secret ingredient'. When it comes to a drip chain lubricant in a bottle, Ceramicspeed uses wax, emulsifiers, a corrosion inhibitor to protect the chain, which it claims not every brand uses, and demineralised water as the carrier, which is what, as the name suggests, helps carry the wax lubricant itself deep into your chain links, where it can do its work and protect the chain. Drip lubricants are mixed thoroughly using machines, heated, and then cooled. Today's formulations are water-based, but the original carrier fluid for the first UFO Drip was kerosene, which was known to melt bottle nozzles over time due to its aggressive nature.The water-based carrier evaporates, leaving behind the wax. Oil-based drip lubricants tend to become dirtier in use because contamination is suspended within the oil, which remains on the chain. Charged with developing CeramicSpeed’s chain lube offerings, Søbjerg Madsen begins by explaining that it’s not possible to have one product that’s the best at everything. “What people need to understand is that there are over 1000 different waxes; there are synthetic and natural products, and each of them has different properties. She explains. “So when sales suggests a new lubricant or a new product, my main goal is to ask, 'What kind of properties do you want?’, because you can't have everything.“The first part is getting the wax composition with the properties that I would like, and once that's done, then I need to find a way to keep it in this water solution, and also get the shelf life correct, and that's a really difficult task.” Søbjerg Madsen explains. A product's composition depends on the desired properties. Is longevity the priority, or is all-out efficiency the goal? Something that lasts for a thousand kilometres may very well not be the fastest option. CeramicSpeed's approach is that a one-size-fits-all product isn't ideal for chain treatments. The first wet lube, for instance, went through 300 experiments to arrive at the desired composition. Cyclists, or at least road cyclists with a focus on performance, often look for what's fastest, or what saves watts, but there's more to it than that. Making a quality product that performs for the most amount of riders, across different regions, climates and weather systems is a tricky ask.CeramicSpeed offers three drip products: All Conditions, Wet, and Indoor and the range was overhauled this year and given a new look.All Conditions and Speed Wax are the best bet for speed; Wet lasts longer and protects your chain in the rain, and Indoor doesn't shed like a regular wax, making it useful for the velodrome or home training. The new Ultra Endurance Wax doesn't focus on low friction, a first for the brand; its priority is high durability and consistent performance over hundreds of kilometres.It is 'stickier'. It might not be the quickest option for a road race, but it will protect a chain for hundreds of kilometres off-road in a gravel race, for example. A super-fast chain wax or lube's benefits will be null and void if it's gone after 2 hours of hard use.The brand's chain lubricants are developed in small batches in the lab and produced in volumes of up to two litres. These samples are used for the brand's testing and by test riders. The brand now also has an in-house production facility where it can produce 50- 300 kg of drip product in a batch, allowing them to control the process. Søbjerg Madsen explains that this close proximity means it can be easy to address issues that may arise from production at scale.“Sometimes, because it's chemistry, and chemistry can be unpredictable when you scale up, we'll see some issues where I have to correct something, then when they say go, they are ready to produce and put it in bottles,” she explains.Shelf life is another factor when it comes to our chain lubricant; top tip: don’t leave the cap off your water-based drip chain wax, as the water will evaporate over time. CeramicSpeed aims for a two-year product shelf life, and needs to ensure a product doesn't solidify in the bottle. Søbjerg Madsen explains that a drip lube which separates in the bottle is a poor sign, something to look for when you are next in the bike shop buying chain lube. "That's a very poor sign; it's a sign that it's unstable, and the product development didn't do a good enough job."Every time I make the sample, I put it in the incubator at 40 degrees. It stays there for three months, and if it doesn't solidify or separate, then we say we have a shelf life of two years," she says. After nearly a decade, it's clear the pair have a strong feel for what's needed, but verification from the test lab's machines and Pedersen's experience and feel inform the direction Søbjerg Madsen needs to take at times. "When I make the first wax compositions, and I think 'Okay, this might be interesting,' then I'll make a test chain for Michael and ask him to do an experiment to measure the watts, because then I have an idea. If it's really high, then I need to do something to make it lower," she explains. The testing lab and three different kinds of sandThe lubricant and wax formulations are designed, and then the testing phase takes around six months on average, though the brand is always busy testing different things, including the competition, and running experiments.Engineer Pedersen has tested a lot of products in general in the lab, including over 800 chains; the 11-speed Shimano Dura-Ace chain is held in particularly high regard. If you are running 11-speed Shimano, buy yourself a Dura-Ace chain.CeramicSpeed uses a combination of internal and external test riders. This includes company founder and CEO Jacob Csizmadia himself; we pass a few of his stealth all-black bikes in the corridor on our way to the lab.The test lab is a fairly small, brightly lit room that is lined with workbenches. Many of which are topped with testing machines, which in different ways all vaguely resemble a bicycle drivetrain. There are five chain testing machines, which all serve a different purpose; There's the original Friction Facts testing machine, a clean conditions test machine, a wet conditions test machine, a machine to add water and sand contaminants together and the brand's latest baby, the Full Load Watt Tester machine (FLWT); a larger unit, which runs as a complete drivetrain, whilst adding sand and water and measuring friction. This machine has been designed to take the brand's testing to the next level. CeramicSpeed measures friction in watts by using torque sensors. The durability of the chain treatment is also monitored, but chain wear specifically is not, though it can be as part of a specific extra-long extreme test.The Friction Facts test machine was the original, weighting a single-speed arrangement at 250 watts of load in a clean environment. It's a style of machine being used by other brands to test as well, but it isn't a full drivetrain and can skew results because the chain is in tension pretty much the whole time due to there being no derailleur.A Tribology test for friction rates called a Pin and Disc test also exists, and whilst it can be performed to an ISO standard, it isn't specific to bicycle drivetrains or modern wax formulas. CeramicSpeed don't consider it to be a worthwhile testing avenue to go down. For years, only clean-conditions testing could be done, but as Søbjerg Madsen points out, unless you are riding in a velodrome environment, "we all know even on a hot summer day, it's not completely clean conditions," meaning dust and other contaminants are still present. A machine that could add contamination was required to mimic real-world conditions. The wet conditions test machine was also developed, but adding only water could only tell so much. "We could only add water, and a lot of water, and what does that really simulate in the real world?" Søbjerg Madsen says. Every cyclist knows a wet, rainy day comes with all sorts of grit, dirt, and mud that also interact with a chain. CeramicSpeed has now developed a machine capable of adding contamination and water. The FLWT machine is run using four different protocols that simulate different conditions over five hours; to standardise things, because, as the pair point out, you could end up just testing forever. These test protocols are as follows:- Clean test without contamination.- Tests with water added every five minutes. - Dry test with sand added every five minutes.- Extreme test with water and sand added every 15 minutes.The brand also uses three different types of sand from around the world in testing because, naturally, it varies all over the world. Sand from Australia, Denmark and America is used. The sands all differ; the one from Colorado in the US is very fine and dusty, the sample from Australia has more clay, and the Danish sand has more 'fine particles'; using it consistently allows for repeatable testing. The FLWT machine uses a motor to power a drivetrain at a load of 250 watts (though this can be altered) and advanced torque sensors on the input and output axles to measure the wattage difference; custom test software has also been written in-house to calculate the test results. CeramicSpeed runs various tests, and the brand was careful not to give me everything; it's a competitive area, so we couldn't dive into all of the test data, graphs and findings. The brand has published some test results on its site for its chain lubricants.Generally, though, tests last five hours, and multiple runs of each test are completed for validation. When test graphs are produced, they show a break in time, an optimal running period and a decline in performance due to wear and/or abrasion from the test contaminants.The FLWT can also be remotely controlled and has a built-in horn to warn colleagues that a test is about to start when the engineers are working remotely.There is even a microphone to monitor the changing sound of a chain's treatment as testing progresses and a lubricant 'wears in'. The sound a chain is making can tell the engineers a lot, and plenty of riders recognise a change in sound as a reminder to re-lube or re-wax their chains. Apparatus in workshops to break in freshly waxed chains is also getting more complex; the brand's advice: re-install your freshly waxed chain, work it by hand a little if needed and go ride it; it will settle down and go quiet soon enough. "We know from the industry that there are a lot of people who are looking into this (an FLWT-style machine), but we have also realised that the problem is getting reproducible data. says Søbjerg Madsen."We really need to be sure that what we are measuring is correct," The team admit that they are still learning the machine, and are aiming to measure very fine differences consistently in order to be as accurate as possible, in part because differences between competitor products are very small. No lubricant test standard exists in the bike industry, and you can't really just go and buy a test machine. This means brands are free to present their testing in whichever way suits them best. "Customers and the companies are saying, 'Well, of course, you're just designing your test to make yours look best,' and that's what everybody is doing, because there is no standard."That's what everybody is doing; they are making their own test, and then, of course, they look best, but what Michael and I are really doing, and it's easy for us to say, is that we are really trying to make tests that mimic the real world. It's much easier to optimise something if you have a standard test to do it," says Søbjerg MadsenThe brand is comparing against the competition, but appears to be doing it fairly, setting up and testing competitor products to spec, as Søbjerg Madsen explains. "If we're doing comparison tests on one of our competitors, we do a lot of work to test it at what they recommend. "We are not just trying to make it look awful. Sometimes we find that, well, this lubricant is actually really good under these conditions, and then, of course, as a chemist and scientist, I'm thinking, 'okay, what do they do that's really good, and how can I optimise mine to get the same performance?"The clue is in the name: with CeramicSpeed, the brand is all about speed and low friction; however, its efforts with chain treatments, drip and hot wax go beyond being able to say 'ours is fastest'. It's a statement the engineers do not make themselves during my visit. Cyclists can make an informed decision on what they might think the best chain product for them is. The brand of drivetrain you run will affect efficiency, as will how well a lubricant is applied and maintained. If you want to maintain the best possible performance, don't skip the re-waxing, cleaning or reapplication, and if that isn't for you, find something that lasts a long time. Though no official industry test standards exist, inter-brand chain lube test result announcements can feel like a fight for supremacy at times. It's clear CeramicSpeed is committed to testing and developing the best possible product. Whilst its product has competitive low-friction or speed levels, there's more to a good chain lube or wax than just being quick.

item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: The Cavaliers did on Wednesday what they do best: win meaningless, regular-season games.The Knicks, meanwhile, handed out a dub and ate a loss on purpose on their way to find their best-working lineups for when winning, you know, actually matters.Here’s the latest from MSG on a rare off day.“We’ll learn from this game, and keep it moving.”On why Bridges remains a starter despite his shooting slump:“Mikal is a starter. And so it’s not a question of that. He’s like a lot of players: They’ve had their good moments and their not so good moments. And Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league.“So, for me to make a quote-unquote ‘panic decision’ and change it right now — we’re 10 games in or whatever we are. I’m not feeling it. So I’m good.”On the Knicks’ defensive physicality and ability to defend without fouling:“Just our level of physicality. Our level of physicality without fouling. Because you can be over the top, grabbing and pushing and holding, but our guys, they’re doing their work early. They’re doing their work early and they’re being real physical about it without putting their hands on guys. When you do that and you do that for close to 48 minutes, you usually get good results. And our guys are doing it.”On the defensive intensity of Landry Shamet and Miles McBride:“I think our physicality on the defensive end of the floor is at a pretty high level. And they [are doing] it the right way. They’re doing it without fouling, which is a lot of fun to watch. The point of attack with Landry and Deuce, especially, on the ball, is unbelievable.”On Josh Hart’s perimeter defense and the importance of his return:“He’s tremendous on the ball. In pick-and-roll situations, we always want our point of confrontation, especially against guys that shoot the ball at the 3-point line, Josh is really good at that. He’s really good at leading with his chest. And he’s strong. He’s a strong guy that knows the league, he knows the players very well.“His impact when it comes to guarding the ball, on the perimeter especially, is something that you always miss.”On the Knicks’ defensive communication, rebounding and improved pick-and-roll coverage:“Their level of communication is high. Their ability to box out is high. Their ability to get back in transition is high. We were hurting in the pick-and-roll game defensively, but we’ve done a better job because the point of attack has been good and our guy guarding the screener has been great, too.”On Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart losing minutes to Shamet and McBride:“It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal. And maybe even at times for Josh. Because those two guys [McBride and Shamet] are playing at a pretty high level.“Part of it is we got two guys that are playing really well in Landry and Deuce. And so it’s hard. It’s going to be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal — and maybe even at times for Josh, because those two guys are playing at a pretty high level, and not just on the offense of the floor but defensively, too.”On the Knicks’ defensive struggles against Cleveland and his decision to keep playing Shamet and McBride:“I mean, this is one of our worst defensive games overall that we’ve had. In the past five or six games we’ve been playing really well at that end of the floor, but they got loose tonight.“And Landry and Deuce have been a big part of what we’ve done defensively. So if they’re playing at a high level, I’ve? got to keep trying to find ways to get those guys on the floor.”On taking responsibility for keeping the Knicks in their defensive blitz against Donovan Mitchell too long:“We blitzed Donovan in the second half and that fourth quarter. Give Donovan credit, he did a nice job making the right play out of it. … I kept us in the blitz a little too long, and I should have taken us out of the blitz. That part is on me.“I kept us in the blitz a little too long. I should have taken us out of the blitz. So that part is on me and I gotta be better helping our group in that area.”On the Knicks’ curious lack of free-throw attempts:“[Cleveland] had 14 more free-throw attempts than us, four more offensive rebounds than us and two less turnovers. When that happens versus a good team, it’s gonna be hard to win the game.“At one time, the free-throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game.”On Brunson receiving no free-throw attempts despite playing nearly 35 minutes:“Jalen plays 34 minutes or almost 35 minutes and he has zero free-throw attempts. That’s pretty alarming. I’m not sure how or why it’s that way. I know at one time, the free throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game. That was part of the reason why we lost the possession game. … James Harden had a great game as well. James shot as many free throws as our whole team.”On Andre Drummond helping replace Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding:“Andre’s done a fantastic job in that area, as an individual. He’s not Mitch, nobody would compare him to Mitch, but he’s brought a dimension to the table that we really like. He’s always been a great offensive rebounder, and he’s showing it now as an individual.”On the Knicks’ assistant coaches emphasizing offensive rebounding and transition defense:“They’re handling the offensive duties and they’ve been emphasizing the crash areas. And they’ve done a great job — a fantastic job — of coaching our group, in that area. So our guys have a really good understanding of when to go and when not to go and how to go so we don’t get beat in transition.”On the Knicks failing to execute in crucial moments against Cleveland:“We were in it. But just timely stops and timely buckets were needed.”On Cleveland’s defensive adjustments and his failure to respond quickly enough:“You gotta give them a lot of credit. It’s something I’ll be a little more prepared for. I just didn’t adjust in-game as fast as I wanted to. I was still able to make plays, but not enough to win.”On needing to be more aggressive even if it means making mistakes:“From how we started the game to how we finished it, just from my end, I can’t be hesitant. I can’t be a little stagnant at times. It puts my team at a disadvantage, so I just have to be more aggressive in my mistakes, if I’m making any. I just need to have a little more aggression.”On supporting Mikal Bridges despite his struggles and criticism from outside the team:“No matter what’s going on, with what people are saying or anything, the people in this room have his back night in and night out. We see the work he puts into his game. We see the time that he puts in. When you’re doing the right things day in and day out, things will eventually fall in your favor. So just giving him support, giving him confidence every single day, regardless of what the noise is on the outside. That’s our brother, and we’re going to keep it that way.”On controlling what he can after receiving no free-throw attempts against Cleveland:“I just gotta control what I can control, and keep it at that.”On taking greater rebounding responsibility following Mitchell Robinson’s departure:“When you lose a great offensive rebounder like Mitchell Robinson, you got to pick up the slack. Of course, we have one of the best rebounders of the generation in Andre Drummond. But I want to do my part, and one of the ways I can impact winning and help our team tremendously on a nightly basis is make sure they don’t get second-chance points and also we get second-chance points.”On the difficulty of defending James Harden after his 32-point performance:“MVP, scoring champ. He’s a tough matchup for anybody in this league. You gotta tip your hat to him.”On the uncalled goaltending on Peyton Watson’s block:“I thought it was a goaltend. The guys behind the bench said that as well.”On James Harden and Donovan Mitchell adjusting to the Knicks’ defensive blitz:“James has been doing this a long time. Donovan’s been doing this a long time. They probably got a little comfortable. At the end of the day, it was a one-possession game, and we could have shored up a few things, probably, that would have helped us keep it a little tighter and given us a chance to win. But give them credit, because they knew what we were doing and took advantage of it.”On his offensive rebounding prowess:“I just got a knack for it.”On the Knicks collectively replacing Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding contributions:“I think a lot of that is effort. And just doing it. A lot of us are crashing. You see guys like Deuce going in for those plays. Everybody, honestly. Picking up where we left off last year. We had a guy (Robinson) who was able to grab a lot of offensive boards, get us extra possessions. So all of us had to kind of step up and do that. But Dre has been doing a great job of rebounding, getting us extra possessions. Kicking it out and finding his way.”

item.title: MET’s New Manta 3 Aero Helmet Promises 6 Free Watts. Here Is What the Data Actually Says.
item.author: Josh Ross
item.content:encoded: The Italian brand finally details the tech behind Tadej Pogačar’s WorldTour helmet. We break down the F1-inspired aero claims, the 250-gram footprint, and why its 5-star safety rating matters more than ever.

item.title: MET Manta 3 review: The all-conquering helmet of the UAE team has finally launched, but just how good is it really?
item.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
item.content:encoded: £299.99 / $375 / €330249g size Medium, 250g claimedSmall, Medium, and LargeAbsolute White, Matte Black, White Black, Glossy Red, Luminous Blue Matte GlossThe MET Manta 3 helmet is not strictly a new helmet. It first broke cover in early 2026 when it was worn on debut by Tadej Pogačar to win yet another monument at Milan-San Remo. Since then, it has been used nearly exclusively by Team UAE-Emirates-XRG, taking the Tour de France yet again, more Monuments, and another men’s World Title this time for Brandon McNulty.Today, however, the helmet officially launches, which means we get to learn a little more about it. We have been testing it on the road in the run-up to launch to see how it performs. Designed using MET’s own wind tunnel, The Tube, with a tagline of ‘Aero is Proven', takes the approach of tangible performance gains, from decreased drag to increased ventilation and reduced weight, all while maintaining safety thanks to in-depth analysis of over 140 crashed helmets.However, the price has also increased, and we have yet to test it ourselves in the wind tunnel to see how it stacks up against the best aero helmets, but initial real-world testing of the helmet so far has been mostly very promising.Design and specificationsThe main design point of the new MET Menta 3 places a heavy focus on aerodynamics. To do this, MET uses its own proprietary wind tunnel, The Tube. This is also the wind tunnel that sponsored teams use for testing new road and time trial helmets with riders to ensure there is good correlation between CFD modelling and then actual on-person testing, something we’ve seen the importance of with our own wind tunnel helmet testing.MET has shared one test figure: 6 watts faster than the old Manta 2, but does not state at what speed this is. Likely 45-50kph given the speeds of WorldTour road races, and these speeds tend to give larger watt differences.MET states that the Manta 3 topped the testing against benchmark competitors. This figure is a reasonable one for those speeds, based on our CN Labs helmet testing as well, and certainly it features a host of design features that lend themselves to strong aero performance. The helmet is narrower and longer than the previous version, and more contoured to divert airflow down the back of the rider rather than create low-pressure turbulence at the rear of the helmet.The helmet looks similar to the likes of the Trek Ballista and Oakley Velo Mach, both helmets that did well in our testing especially when fitted to a rider model in a more aggressive breakaway position. However, this helmet features noticeably more vents than these options. Ventilation was another key target for MET; it states the new Manta has 10% better ventilation than the predecessor.Apparantly this was tested using a thermal viewer and capture system with a copper-coated head model. No further details were provided, as that likely covers some trade secrets.This increased ventilation comes from more frontal vents, the new brow vent borrowed from the Trenta Gen 2, and greater channelling internally into exhausts. This is a similar system to the POC Procen Air, which I find very well-vented at speed thanks to inlets and large channels inside. MET uses a double deck at the rear of the helmet, both to increase the airflow and heat exhaustion, and to help channel that air over the back of the rider.Safety is also key here, with the helmet getting a 5-star Virginia Tech Helmet Lab rating. MIPS Air Node Pro is used inside for rotational impact protection, and it also helps keep the weight low at 250g claimed for a medium, 249g on our scales. All the EPS foam is also wrapped and protected by the polycarbonate shell, while the Safe-T fit system ensures a secure fit around the head and across the cradle and straps. To test the safety of the helmet, 142 crashed helmets from sponsored teams were analysed, along with 745 test impacts across different angles and velocities, and counting.At present, colour options include matte back, absolute white, gloss red, and team colourways. Sizes are S, M and L. DualGel front pad and USB LED light are additional accessories that can be purchased separately.Something I really wasn’t a fan of with the previous generation Manta was that the helmet felt to be rather tight on the sides of my head. I also found this on the first-generation Trenta. With the latest Manta, I am glad to say that the fit has been greatly improved, and it is a lot less narrow on the sides relative to the length. It does this while still incorporating MIPS technology in the form of Air Node. This is widely used across a lot of road helmets now and has a good reputation for getting a good score in the Virginia Tech Helmet Safety Rating. Indeed, the new Trenta helmet is one of the highest-scoring road helmets that has been tested there and features similar technology.Testing the helmet, the hot weather of the summer has gone, but there have still been a few days with low 20°C temperatures to test out the ventilation. Having had a helmet sent to test in the matte Black colour, there is a degree of heat radiation absorption, and the helmet does get warm to the touch in indirect sunlight. I much prefer helmets in light colour options for this reason. However, the ventilation is greatly improved compared to the previous helmet. The front vents are larger, while the internal channelling is deeper to allow for a greater degree of movement of air within the helmet. This also means that at speed there is a good amount of hot air that exits the rear in the exhaust vents. This effect is most felt at speeds above 35 km an hour, though, with professional road racing speeds of 45 km an hour making this helmet incredibly airy. However, at lower speeds with reduced airflow, the lack of vents on the top of the helmet does mean that it can get quite stuffy, especially when climbing at low speeds and high outputs. This is a helmet designed to go fast.Another new feature is the brow venting, as seen on the new Trenta helmet. It does a good job at reducing the amount of heat buildup around your forehead, but being someone who runs quite warm, I still found the over longer rides I had sweat dripping into my eyes. At present, the only helmets that have eliminated this are the Giro Eclipse Pro and Aries, as the brow pad padding features a silicone bead which diverts the sweat to the side of your face. However, MET does state that a MET DualGel front pad is available; I have not tested this yet, but a gel design may help disperse sweat to the side of the brow and away from the eyes.In terms of the aerodynamic performance, it is difficult to say, as we have yet to test this helmet in the wind tunnel. Going off the features that have been implemented, these are designed methodologies that have been used across a broad array of different aero helmets that have tested well. Featuring large vents at the front combined with deep channels internally towards the exhausts has tended to reduce the pressure drag off the back of the rider’s helmet. Another feature that tends to work well is a fairly narrow profile, especially for riders who ride with their head in a more upright position, as it reduces the frontal area. The shape of the helmet and the venting is also similar to the Trek Ballista, with the rear vents positioned in a way that should help direct airflow over the back when in a more aggressive position.Certainly, the performance of the helmet has not slowed down the professional riders who have been using it, but that is not a very good judge of performance given that Pogačar could probably be in a commuter helmet and still win.The helmet has been designed using MET’s in-house wind tunnel, The Tube. Personally, I have no reason to doubt that the helmet is a strong performer. But as we have seen in our own testing, the performance of the helmet will likely vary compared to others based on the position of the rider using it.For a more subjective measurement, the helmet is impressively light. It’s not as light as the POC Cytal Lite, but it does compare very favourably to many other aero helmets. For those wanting to reduce total system weight by as much as possible while maintaining aerodynamic performance, this helmet is a very strong contender.I have also been using it for very long days in the saddle, and it’s been exceptionally comfortable. The padding is well distributed throughout, and the straps have a good range of adjustment. The rear cradle adjustment is also very welcome, and the dial is easy to use. There are vents at the side that are designed to be able to house glasses when not wearing them; however, I found that not many glasses worked with these helmets. Quite often the arm was a bit too thick and wouldn’t lodge into them. Scicon glasses, coincidentally used alongside MET by sponsored WorldTour teams, do fit well because they have very slim arms. POC, Oakley, and AlbaOptics fitted less well.Unfortunately, with all these new aero features, reduced weight, and increased ventilation, the price of the helmet has now jumped up. The previous helmet was £229.99 at RRP, often dipping into the £150 region online; the new helmet starts at £299.99 / $375 and places it in the same ballpark as the Giro Eclipse Pro, Specialized Evade 4, Fizik Kudo, Oakley Velo Mach, Sweet Protection Tucker III 2Vi and Ekoi R-Aero.There are of course cheaper offerings, with the Trek Ballista and HJC Furion 3 being closer to the £200 /$250 bracket, while the Van Rysel RCR-F helmet remains a relative outlier at £129.99. But that shouldn’t be an outlier, and hopefully pressure brands to stop pushing prices higher and higher. Yes, wind tunnel testing and development is not cheap, but the RCR-F is a strong aero performer, so we know good aero helmets can be made and sold for less.Compared to the competition, until we test the Manta 3 in the tunnel, we can’t categorically say how it compares. I can say from my own testing that ventilation is better than the Sweet Protection, and at speed, better than the Giro. However, the Giro brow padding prevents sweat from getting into my eyes. The MET, though, is lighter. It really balances out somewhat evenly between the MET and the Giro for me, but I lean towards the Giro in warmer weather for the brow padding and white colour, while I lean towards the MET in cooler conditions and when speed is the focus. If I were buying on a budget, I would still go for the Van Rysel and recommend that helmet to anyone who wants the best value-for-money aero helmet.The MET Menta 3 is a full revolution of the previous Manta, while adding some fantastic features from the featherweight, airy Trenta Gen 2.The new helmet is lighter, far better ventilated, and promises to be more aerodynamic as well. I can’t categorically comment on that last one, but many of the designed features implemented suggest it is a faster helmet for racing speeds.It still relies on high speeds and more airflow for peak ventilation, so low-speed climbing can get more stuffy. While the glasses docking is not the best, it is also not necessary. It does, however, cost a lot; I would have liked to see the inclusion of the gel padding, as well as a rear light as standard, to help justify a price hike of nearly 30% over the previous version. I personally love the sleek look of the helmet, with the absolute white colourway looking great as well as this matte black, but gloss is better for avoiding marks. Drops one point for average glasses docking, but that isn’t weighted heavily as it renders an aero helmet not very aero so you shouldn’t do it.I would prefer a gel padding that avoids sweat dripping in the eyes as with Giro helmets, and that option may be available but not as standard with the MET. Otherwise the helmet fits very well and works well with many different glasses.At speed, the helmet is downright airy and in winter weather it’s been very cool. However, at low speeds and high effort, it can get warm, but so does virtually every good aero helmet. The black colour also heats up in direct sunlight, so white is a smarter choice.Heavily crash tested, latest MIPS tech, good retention system, and a 5/5 VTH rating mean there is nothing I can criticise here.We haven’t tested the helmet yet, but there is likely a good reason sponsored teams almost ditched the Trenta to race exclusively in the new Manta even in hot weather, so important is the aero advantage. It uses many tried and tested features and technologies that should ensure solid aero performance.£300 is not cheap, but annoyingly is becoming something of the norm for top of the range aero road helmets. If it came with the gel padding and rear light as standard, it would score better, at present it is only beaten in price by a small handful of £300+ helmets, but sits in the same region as the Giro, Oakley, and Specialized competitors.

item.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Max Fried
item.author: John Griffin
item.content:encoded: When Max Fried signed an eight-year, $218 million contract during the 2024-2025 offseason, the scouting report said that the Yankees were getting one of the game’s premier southpaws with impeccable defense, but who had regularly battled injuries throughout his career. Now at the contract’s quarter pole, that scouting report has played out as advertised. Across his first two years in pinstripes, Fried’s 8.3 fWAR and 2.83 ERA rank eighth and fifth, respectively, among starters with at least 300 innings pitched, and he took home the 2025 AL Gold Glove. After a mostly healthy 2025 that saw him throw a career-high 195 innings, however, the 32-year-old battled injuries this season, culminating in an offseason elbow surgery announced earlier this week. 20 starts, 112.2 IP, 2.80 ERA (150 ERA+), 2.65 FIP, 3.59 xFIP, 24.0 K%, 7.6 BB%, 3.5 fWAR, 3.7 rWAR Entering third year of eight-year, $218 million contractWith Ace of the Past Gerrit Cole still rehabbing from Tommy John surgery and Ace of the Future Cam Schlittler about to explode on the scene, Fried was tabbed as the Yankees’ Opening Day starter in San Francisco — his fourth career Opening Day start, and first in pinstripes. He was characteristically dominant in that first start, allowing just two runs in 6.1 scoreless frames to set the tone not just for his 2026 performance, but that of the Yankees’ rotation as a whole.When healthy this season, Fried was the definition of consistency. Across his 20 regular season starts, he allowed more than three runs just three times. One came against the LA Angels on April 16th, during that strange four-game set in the Bronx where the Yankees’ pitching staff randomly crumbled to pieces (they gave up 32 total runs against the American League’s second-worst offense). The second came on May 8th, where the future World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers put together a four-run second inning courtesy of four singles and a pair of walks; since he would hit the injured list with an elbow bruise following his next start, it’s fair to wonder whether he was beginning to feel the effects of the injury here. The third, and final, came in the final week of the season, as the Rays offense broke through in the seventh as he was outdueled by Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen. Even in these three starts, however, Fried managed to give the Yankees length, going 5.1, 6, and 6.1 innings in each, respectively.In his other 17 outings, Fried was magnificent. He surrendered one run or fewer in 12 of those outings, and struck out six or more nine times. More importantly, he continued to be elite at generating soft contact, ranking in the 99th percentile in barrel percentage, 97th percentile in hard hit percentage, 96th percentile in average exit velocity, and 83rd percentile in ground ball percentage. Furthermore, when the lights shone brightest, Fried came up big. Taking the ball against Boston in Game 2 of the Wild Card Round, he spun six innings of one-run ball, striking out six and walking just one; the only blemish came on a Willson Contreras home run with two outs in the sixth, a wall-scraper that was Boston’s first postseason run since the sixth inning of Game 2 of the previous year’s Wild Card Round. He wasn’t quite as strong a week later, getting tagged with the loss as the Yankees got swept, but honestly, he pitched well enough to keep the Yankees in the ballgame: in truth, he really only made two bad pitches all night, although both unfortunately ended up in the seats.As we look ahead to next season, there is a concern on the horizon: Fried’s injury history. As we know, elbows are a ticking time bomb for pitchers, even those like Fried who rely less on swing-and-miss stuff and more on soft contact. Even though Fried is on track to be a full go for the hypothetical spring training that starts on time, and will almost certainly be ready for whenever the teams actually report, we’re still going to want to keep an eye on his elbow going forward. That’s true for all pitchers, though, and at least with Fried, we know that, when he’s on the mound, he’s going to be an ace.See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here.

item.title: 'The most tradable sport nobody trades': Inside race prediction platform RPM
item.author: The Race Media
item.content:encoded: RPM is the world’s first motorsport prediction platform, where every outcome of a race event becomes a tradable market. Fans are able to buy and sell outcomes on every moment of a race at a moment’s notice.Founder Ben Jarrett joined The Race Business as part of our Spotlight series of interviews to explain how he spotted a niche in the motorsport market - and how RPM itself could play a part in changing how fans consume motorsport.“RPM is at the intersection of motorsport, content creation, and prediction markets,” says Jarrett.Will it rain? Who pits first? Which tyres do they choose? Fans can essentially make predictions about every single facet of motorsport. And it’s an idea that was born out of a racetrack. “I was racing GT4 cars, and I’m standing on the pitwall. Someone comes up and says: ‘10 bucks, he puts it into the wall at Turn 1’. “The other guy’s like, ‘No, no, 100 bucks, he puts it [into the wall]’.“Everyone was standing there. I was in my suit, I had my hands on my helmet, and we were supposed to go out there for practice before qualifying and put a lap in.”It was at that moment that Jarrett had the idea to open up motorsport prediction markets to fans and content creators.“I handed in my HANS device and my helmet to my mate and I drove home.”He says the RPM app is as “simple as having a question that you want a large fanbase to help you solve. That’s a market: Max Verstappen to win in Australia, George Russell to make a pass for the lead on lap 10, or whenever”.Jarrett says he’s found a gap in the market as motorsport fans don’t traditionally engage in iGaming - wagering on outcomes online - as other sports fans do, with football and basketball being the most popular sports in this regard.“I would say there are 1.3 billion fans of motorsport. But in terms of iGaming volume, it provides less than half a percent. “So, it's one of the most tradable sports on earth that nobody trades, that nobody touches. “There are 72 days a year that F1 is on, and it’s becoming a part of people’s daily life.”He points us to F1’s Global Fan Survey that, in 2025, found that 61% of motorsport fans engage with F1 content on a daily basis. “So, this is a fan ecosystem that really is becoming part of people's daily life. And if we go and we look at social media… motorsport content is everywhere.”RPM is also geared towards giving content creators their own space. Creators can build a standalone competition around an event - or keep the competition running all season with a running leaderboard - while RPM handles the predictions, scoring, credits, prizing support and league access.Approved creators can even unlock revenue share opportunities with RPM in the future. “I'm very interested in the content creators. And we use that word a lot because that's where we really see the opportunity. We want to give them a voice. We want to give them participation.“We don't just see them as like a marketing push. We really see them as part of the heartbeat of what is RPM. This is a platform for them to come in, engage in motorsport on a daily basis, through markets, in a different way.”

item.title: Mathieu van der Poel's coach and father still in the dark over cyclo-cross participation this winter
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: There is still a sense of mystery surrounding Mathieu van der Poel's cyclo-cross season, with the Dutch national coach saying he still doesn't know whether the star man will compete this winter and that Van der Poel's father doesn't, either. Van der Poel has been a dominant force in cyclo-cross over the course of his career, winning eight world titles, but he has not yet committed to returning to the discipline this winter. He is due to become a father in January, which is clearly a factor, and while he has not yet ruled out racing, he has not confirmed any plans so far, with the World Cup series starting in two weeks' time."I’m curious too," Van der Poel's national coach for cyclo-cross and mountain bike, Gerben de Knegt said this week on the Live Slow Ride Fast podcast of fellow Dutchmen Laurens ten Dam and Stefan Bolt. "I’ve even asked [Van der Poel's father] Adrie about it, but he doesn’t know either."Bolt, seeing the funny side, then chimed in: "Adrie is just as in the dark as the rest of us. It’s quite funny, really. People interview Adrie as if he has some special insight into Mathieu’s life."De Knegt also highlighted Van der Poel's impending fatherhood, which is set to come in the middle of the season, in the same month as the World Championships, which take place right at the end of January. "Of course, there’s the family aspect, when it comes to the idea of not doing any 'cross this winter. Well, given that he’s going to be a dad around January, this is actually the ideal winter to skip it," De Knegt said. As for the possibility of dropping in just for the World Championships, he said: "I’ve discussed that with him often in the past. But it's not really an option. We’ve always preferred to do more races."Van der Poel himself has hinted in the past that he could skip cyclo-cross entirely one winter. After collecting his eighth world title in February earlier this year, he said: "Maybe it's not a bad idea to skip one winter because to be here it's the first peak of my season always, not only physically, but also mentally. "This is a day when I want to be in top shape, 90% is not enough or would not be enough for me to be at the start line here."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
