item.title: Who had the biggest breakout performances in the world of gravel in 2026? Here are six riders with top form through clouds of dust and mires of mud
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: The spotlight of gravel and mountain bike racing always shines on familiar performers like Keegan Swenson, Sofia Gomez Villafañe, Mads Würtz Schmidt, Kate Courtney and two-time gravel world champion Marianne Vos. They line up at an off-road race, and people pay attention. However, deeper fields around the world now challenge these proven winners, coming from various backgrounds and fresh talent has made impressive moves to grab attention, especially at events in the UCI Gravel World Series, Gravel Earth Series and Life Time Grand Prix.This year's UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, the first time in five years rainbow stripes were decided outside Europe, saw a gravel specialist win the men's race, Magnus Bak Klaris of Denmark. Of course, Vos reigns on all surfaces, but she was put to the test by Rosa Klöser, Larissa Hartog and Nele Laing, women who focus on dirt racing.Because of the distance and cost to travel to Western Australia, as well as a conflict with Little Sugar MTB in Arkansas for many Life Time Grand Prix riders, some of the breakout rides happened long before races for rainbow stripes. The Traka continued to provide a platform for new stars, while Unbound Gravel always has storylines, during the mudfest itself and in the days following, like riders jumping into iconic US one-day races like Tulsa Tough or winning an unexpected US road title. Who went from a supporting role to a leading role this season? Who was able to score a career-defining victory or podium?Here is a collection of notable athletes we noticed from the 2026 calendar of off-road racing.Magnus Bak Klaris certainly wasn't a rider off the gravel radar before 2026, with multiple Danish National Gravel Championships wins plus victories that included Santa Vall, The Rift and the UCI World Series race Wörthersee Gravel. However, at races like The Traka and Unbound, where the prestige and attention hit another level, Bak Klaris hadn't cut through to the podium step, plus his early-season results in 2026 weren't quite what they had been last season. The 30-year-old rider, however, had certainly turned that around before 2026 was over. The signs of the building form were on display in September, when the previously missing season win tally started to build at Falling Leaves Lahti and then continued to roll on at Gravel Grit n' Grind. Still, even though he had finished in the top 10 at the UCI Gravel World Series in 2026, that was not enough to make him among the heavily marked men of the rainbow jersey race, which worked to his advantage. "I didn't come in as one of the favourites, so I could maybe save some more energy than some of the others and hide a little bit," he told a small group of media, including following the event. That 'little bit' was enough to help propel him in the four-man sprint and claim a win that means he'll not be able to hide in the pack through 2027, not with the rainbow jersey on his back. (SG)A one-time Zwift Academy finalist, Nele Laing entered the 2026 season with some promising gravel results after stepping into a few races in the UCI Gravel World Series and coming just off the podium at two of them. Though when she ventured over to the United States, now with the Canyon-DT Swiss squad, to try her hand at Sea Otter, she was definitely the wild card in the leading group of four that charged toward the line. Impressive enough was her presence in Monterey alongside three-time US gravel champion Lauren Stephens (Aegis x Land of Enchantment), 2025 Traka 360 and Unbound 200 winner Karolina Migoń (PAS Racing) and the now four-time Life Time Grand Prix series winner Sofia Gomez Villafañe (Specialized Off-road). However, she wasn't just holding on but was the first of the four to put on the pressure through the crucial final section, and dropped Migoń as a result. Villafañe may have ultimately come over the top with Stephens following, but third at that early-season US race was more than enough to make sure she wouldn't be able to go unnoticed. The 27-year-old then clearly showed that this was more than a one-off with third at The Traka, wins at UCI series events Hegau and 3Rides, plus a fourth at the UCI Gravel World Championships. Then, in a result that will help ensure she is keenly watched by rivals in 2027, she finished off the season by winning Nedbank Gravel Burn. (SG)Victories define seasons for athletes, and one win stands out the most in 2026 for Bradyn Lange. Yes, he did win Sea Otter Classic Gravel in the stars-and-stripes jersey to take the top spot in the opening round of the Life Time Grand Prix. But it was how he won, out-sprinting four-time race winner Keegan Swenson with a crafty move on the final corner. Lange proved his decision in 2025 to focus solely on gravel, or "try to be one of the best at one thing instead of good at multiple", was working. He won his first US national title in any discipline on the gravel roads of Minnesota. He moved to Canyon x DT Swiss ATR for the new year and won The Hills, a UCI Gravel World Series event in Italy, then finished second at The Traka 200 in Spain, and beat the best off-road rider in California.The Oregon native still exhibited his mountain bike prowess with podiums at Leadville Trail 100 MTB and Chequamegon MTB, boosting him to his best finish in the Grand Prix across five years, finishing fifth on the elite men's leaderboard. He had the unique distinction of being the youngest rider in the Grand Prix field back in 2022 at age 21. Now at 27, he's got an early invitation to return for a sixth season, and he can no longer ride under the radar. (JT)"A surreal experience" is how Kylee Hanel described making the main chase group at Big Sugar Gravel to finish fourth overall. While Stella Hobbs rode away with the solo victory, the 20-year-old held her own against the most dominant riders in off-road racing, Sofia Gomez Villafañe and Hayley Preen taking the final podium spots, while Hanel held off a charging Karolina Migoń. She sealed the women's U23 title in the Life Time Grand Prix with top series points in all the races except Leadville Trail 100 MTB, where she finished second in the category. In between Sea Otter Gravel and the overall win at Unbound Gravel 100, she went back on the road with Aegis x LOE and went fourth overall at Tour of the Gila, with a stage win and youth classification title.The multi-talented rider from Oregon competed for the first time at national events last year, where she had top 10s at US road and gravel nationals. Then this summer, she won the USPro U23 women's time trial national championship by 36 seconds over her closest competitor. She didn't realise at the time that it qualified her for Road Worlds, but knew it was a great opportunity for experience and to ride for Team USA in Montreal, even with two more Grand Prix races to follow in October."I'm the only one putting pressure on myself," she admitted to at the UCI Road World Championships, finishing 21st in the U23 time trial and 29th in the road race. The pressure was off when she landed on the wide-angle podium at Big Sugar. (JT)Matthew Wilson may have been in the Life Time Grand Prix in 2025, but he walked away from last year with 'unfinished business' after not delivering the hoped-for results. With a new team in 2026, Scott Sports USA-Shimano, and determination to show what he was really capable of, Wilson went all out in pursuit of a wild card spot this year. The rider from New Zealand gained that spot, with 12th at Sea Otter Gravel and 28th at Unbound, but this time the best was yet to come. Some indication of his early season form was already on display when the multi-discipline rider, who had come third at the New Zealand National Championships road race at the start of the year, washed off the mud of Kansas, borrowed a mate's road wheels and went straight to the top of a criterium podium at Tulsa Tough. Then, when he shifted into his mountain bike comfort zone at Leadville, his LifeTime journey all of a sudden took on a whole new complexion. Wilson went from fighting for a start in the series to fighting for the top spots with his Leadville Trail 100 MTB runner-up spot and then a win at Chequamegon. Fifth at the season-ending Big Sugar Gravel was enough for a third-place overall and to clinch a guaranteed spot in 2026. There is now no doubting what the 25-year-old is truly capable of. (SG)Martins Blums gained entry into this year's Life Time Grand Prix as a wild card with top finishes at Sea Otter Gravel and Unbound Gravel 200. A 12-time mountain champion of Latvia, including the 2024 Marathon MTB national title, Blums was in the chase group behind winner Matthew Wilsom at Chequamegon MTB and finished eighth. He then surprised the field in second overall at Big Sugar Gravel, where he surged from 12th to seventh overall in the final series standings.Big Sugar was indeed big for his 31st birthday, racing with bib number 31. He made a breakaway group after backtracking from a wrong turn, finished on the podium in second place, and, with a series top-10 finish, earned his ticket to return in 2027. He had limited gravel racing in his legs when he started at Sea Otter Gravel in California, but had support for his solo season from Scott Sport USA. Unbound was unfamiliar territory, which he said made him nervous, "but at the same time, it will be a cool challenge," he admitted on a social post. A knee injury at a World Cup mountain bike race in Switzerland kept him away from Leadville Trail 100 MTB, so we'll have to wait another year to see if his precision on a mountain bike can give Keegan Swenson a run for his money. (JT)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Superprestige Niel: Manon Bakker masters the mud to take the win
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Manon Bakker took her first Superrestige series win on Wednesday, the Velosport Veluwe rider dominating the race, riding alone to take the victory at the Jaarmarktcross in Niel.Bakker escaped on the second of the five laps of the muddy course, eking out a lead and holding it. She eventually crossed the line 14 seconds ahead of Italian champion Sara Casasola (Crelan-Corendon) in second, with Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen) third.The race was notable for the abandon of World Champion Lucinda Brand, the Baloise-Poetsbureau Lions rider crashing out on the opening lap.With Bakker well ahead early on in the race, the day became a huge battle for the podium places, with Betsema edging clear first before Casasola launched her bid to close down Bakker late in the piece.Bakker has had an excellent start to the year, opening her 2026/27 by winning six North American races from eight starts before returning to Europe for her first season riding as a privateer, running her own team.In conditions which suited her to the ground, Bakker rode an almost flawless race, building her advantage quickly and defending brilliantly, slipping over only once, in the thick mud.The third round of the season-long Superprestige series, the annual Jaarmarktcross in Niel, was held over five laps of a varied course, with plenty of sand, a series of what look like moguls, short sharp climbs, run-ups and plenty of mud.The first sand pit came early in the lap, and, with none of the riders able to ride it, the bunch was spread in the first few hundred metres. Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) exited in first place, and with teammate Leonie Bentveld behind her, the French rider quickly had a gap.After winning the European title in controversial circumstances, Brand set off in pursuit. However, on one of the many short climbs she hit the barrier and was forced to retire from the race with an injury to her ankle.As Brand rode back to her team camper, Fouquenet was caught, with Aniek van Alphen (777TV) and Bakker briefly gapping the two Pauwels Sauzen riders.However, as the second lap wore on, the in-form Bakker, fresh from a clutch of race victories in North America, rode clear, taking a lead of 18 seconds into lap three ahead of an expanded six-woman chasing group.At the end of the third lap, she had lost only one second of that advantage, with Betsema and Casasola beginning to eat away at the lead. On the final lap, Casasola dropped Betsema and began to pressure Bakker, closing in, almost to within touching distance, but the Dutch rider held her nerve and form to take the win.Sara Casasola (Ita) Crelan-CorendonDenise Betsema (Ned) De Ceuster BouwkranenLeonie Bentveld (Ned) Pauwels Sauzen-Altez IndustriebouwAniek van Alphen (Ned) 777TV CX TeamAmandine Fouquenet (Fra) Pauwels Sauzen-Altez IndustriebouwInge van der Heijden (Ned) Crelan-CorendonHélène Clauzel (Fra) 777TV CX TeamJulie Brouwers (Bel) Charles Liégeois CX TeamRebecca Gariboldi (Ita) De Ceuster BouwkranenLauren Molengraaf (Ned) 777TV CX TeamZita Peeters (Bel) De Ceuster BouwkranenAnn-Christine Allik (Est)

item.title: 'Increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists' – Garmin partners with navigation app Waze to increase rider safety with real-time alerts
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Bike tech company Garmin has announced a partnership with the user-based navigation app, Waze, to provide drivers using the app with real-time locations of riders.It’s hoped the collaboration will increase rider safety, with drivers alerted to the presence of cyclists and better informed to slow down and take appropriate action. "By bringing Live Cycling Alerts to Waze, we’re giving drivers a helpful heads-up so they can slow down, stay aware and safely share the road," said Waze VP and GM, Gai Berkovich.The system works when riders using one of Garmin’s compatible bike computers, like the new suite of Edge devices, or smartwatches activate the LiveTrack feature, using the Garmin Connect app on a smartphone. While this was created to allow riders the ability to share location, planned route and other features with family and friends, this now extends to the partnership with Waze."This collaboration brings greater peace of mind to cyclists by extending the benefit of LiveTrack to motorists using Waze for greater awareness of their surroundings," read the Garmin press release."Location sharing is temporary and session-based, and the cyclist’s personal information will not be shared or displayed in Waze." It also applies only to outdoor cycling activities.Instead, what Waze users will see are 'Live Cycling Alerts' informing drivers of the cyclist’s presence on the road, with rider icons moving on the road in their vicinity."Garmin is well-known in the cycling industry for its safety-focused products and features, and we are excited to work with Waze to bring this unique feature to cyclists and drivers alike," said Garmin’s Vice President of Consumer Sales and Marketing, Susan Lyman."By increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists, this new tool is designed to foster a safer riding environment for Garmin customers by giving drivers valuable real-time visibility to their whereabouts, helping to create a more connected experience for everyone on the road."Waze was created in 2009 as a community-based navigation application, which employs its users' generated travel information to provide the best navigation options.What do you think? Will you activate this feature on your Garmin, can it really make your ride safer? Let us know in the comments.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: What we know about worrying new Honda F1 reliability issue
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Honda's worrying return of reliability problems includes a new issue, the root cause of which it might not trace before the end of the Formula 1 season.Aston Martin and engine partner Honda suffered their third DNF of the triple-header in Brazil, when Lance Stroll retired for the second race in a row.Stroll had two separate battery problems over the course of the Brazil weekend and didn't make it to mid-distance in Sunday's grand prix.It means Stroll has finished just six of the 20 races held this season, while team-mate Fernando Alonso has had seven retirements of his own.There have been some flashes of optimism - in relative terms, given how disastrous this first season of the new alliance has been - of late as Alonso scored points in Malaysia five races ago, had surprisingly good pace at Austin despite sustaining significant floor damage on the opening lap, and excelled in the wet in Brazil.There, Alonso comfortably gave Aston Martin and Honda their best qualifying of the year, getting into Q3 for the first time and lining up eighth on the grid.But this has been badly undercut by a return of significant fragility that's closer to how badly Honda started 2026.Reliability problems also put paid to Alonso's chances in Mexico, where he had looked quite competitive and closer to the top 10 than normal. The issue was related to the cooling system inside the energy recovery system, whereas in Brazil the emergence of battery problems for Stroll sounded a clear alarm bell.Shintaro Orihara, Honda's lead trackside engineer, acknowledged that "we know what happened, but we don't know what is the root cause".He admitted it may take a few weeks to find that, but already from the data there needs to be some kind of countermeasure for the next race in Las Vegas, while Honda traces the underlying cause so it can be addressed properly for 2027."We need to find the actual root cause of this error for next year," he said."Otherwise, we keep having the same issue."This was a different kind of failure to what had occurred in Mexico, which had led to MGU-K problems. But the theme is similar: in Mexico, Orihara had admitted to a lack of robustness within Honda's engine in more ways than one, and the fault there hadn't shown up in simulation.Now Honda knows what happened but doesn't know why. That's a worrying through-line between the two issues. It also harks back to the start of the year, when Honda could identify the obvious catastrophic consequences of the problems that were emerging and could see broadly where they came from, but didn't know exactly what the problem's root was, because it had come out of the blue compared with what it had experienced on the dyno.What's particularly alarming is that this does seem to be a regression from where Honda had got to in the middle of the season.Its performance was obviously still lacking, and its engine is still underpowered on the internal combustion side, even with upgrades through the year to try to trim the deficit.But it had at least got to a point where its cars were finishing races, which allowed Alonso to score some points when the Aston Martin was heavily upgraded.Either side of the summer break, Alonso had five straight finishes, and Stroll got two of his six finishes this year in three races before the summer break too.Orihara acknowledged that reliability was simply better in the middle of the season, but that has been replaced by "several issues" in recent races.Some of this trend could be related to the mileage of parts - components simply coming to the end of their life cycle - or to just a case of Honda trying to run the engine harder for performance and going over the edge.But with the battery issue that emerged in Brazil specifically, it's too early to say what the trigger was.Honda has not made the progress it would have hoped for this season in terms of the all-round performance of the engine, and at best has only achieved some of its performance targets in very specific circumstances.So the fact that reliability has got worse, without a clear upside, puts Honda under pressure and brings an unfortunate amount of negative scrutiny again, right at the end of a year in which it has had to come through quite a lot of adversity.It is also a curveball for the development work Honda is doing on 2027, when it needs to take a step in both performance and reliability.Everything that has been indicated so far is that there will not be a major step at the start of the new season. There's already a plan to phase in further upgrades through the year. But that work will already be deeply under way.Troubleshooting takes away human resource, limited dyno hours which are restricted under F1's engine development limits, money that comes under the engine cost cap, and simply time because the clock is ticking to the start of 2027.First the cooling issue in Mexico, whatever that was exactly, and now this on the battery side, takes Honda's focus away from a path that it would ideally be a lot further down.Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe was in Brazil, which Orihara said has a galvanising effect on the staff - "but on the other hand, we had a battery issue twice this weekend".It was not exactly how Honda's F1 operation would have liked to present itself in front of the big boss. But, as Orihara noted, Mibe at least "knows what is happening trackside"."He will bring this experience to the Japanese side and also boost our development," said Orihara.If there was ever any possibility of complacency creeping in about how much work Honda has to do to reach the necessary standard, the CEO seeing first-hand the kind of problems still being encountered this deep into 2026 will have stamped it out.

item.title: 'I continued even after I thought it was fun' – Former U23 world champion retires aged 27
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Five years ago, Johan Price-Pejtersen looked to be on the verge of a highly successful career as a professional cyclist, but it is now fizzling out at the age of just 27. The Danish rider claimed the U23 time trial world champion in Bruges in 2021, to go alongside his Danish and European titles. Beating Luke Plapp and Florian Vermeersch in Bruges, he announced himself as a future star and, though he did already have a professional contract with Uno-X, earned a move to the WorldTour with Bahrain Victorious. After three years with that team, Price-Pejtesen spent the past two years with Alpecin-Premier Tech, but has decided to hang up his wheels at the end of 2026. "It's an upheaval, but it's also a decision I made quite a long time ago," the 27-year-old said on the Danish Forhjulslir podcast. "When you've been in cycling for a long time, you gain some experience. I've always said: 'I'll keep going until I don't think it's fun anymore'. Some things sound noble in the moment. The fact is that I continued riding my bike even after I thought it was fun."As well as losing the passion for the sport, Price-Pejtersen also suggested he encountered physical problems that held him back."I had a period of two months where every time I went out to train, I felt like I had eaten something bad for breakfast, like I was going to throw up," he said. "It's strange, but also true. I've spent some time thinking about it and getting used to it."No pro win, controversiallyPrice-Pejtersen has raced sparingly since making his first and only Grand Tour appearance at this year's Giro d'Italia, where he placed a notable seventh in the time trial. Since May he has only completed 10 race days, all on Danish soil, winding down his career with a final pro-level appearance at the Tour of Denmark followed by two criterium races. Price-Pejtersen largely slotted into a domestique role over the years, and while he did achieve some strong results against the clock – including podiums at Tirreno-Adriatico and the Chrono des Nations – he never managed to win a race during his career. item.title: 'We are certainly not doomed' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team in mid-season sponsor search after co-title sponsor pulls out
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team will be searching for a new title sponsor as Glowi, owner of cleaning agency Het Poetsbureau, is set to withdraw from its sponsorship deal at the end of this year.Glowi took up a multi-year co-sponsorship of the team at the start of 2025, but the company had an option to withdraw at the end of each year."That option has now been exercised," Sven Nys, who runs the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions team, told Belgian newspaper .The team currently have eight riders on their roster across the men's and women's elite and under-23 ranks, including recently-crowned European champions Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand, and Annemarie Worst and Pim Ronhaar.Thibau's father Sven said Glowi's decision to withdraw from sponsorship is unrelated to team results. reports that the company is facing its own difficulties."We built an incredibly good relationship with the people from Glowi and Het Poetsbureau, where I myself used to give cycling clinics to cleaning staff in all provinces. They were happy with our performance, and we gave them enormous visibility," Nys said."[The decision] is also completely unrelated to our team. They made a decision, and we respect it."The team will continue with Baloise on board until the end of the 2027-28 cyclo-cross season, though they're now searching for a new co-title sponsor, with a contract set to begin mid-season."At a more difficult time for us than for a road team. Because we are in the middle of a cyclo-cross season and the contracts run until January 1. That leaves us in a tight spot," Nys said."In 2026, that applies to cycling in general and to every team looking for potential new partners. Unfortunately, in this sport, you are never all set."Companies that believe in us and 'want' to invest are our only income. It is a constant matter of keeping your feelers out. Discussions are ongoing. But you don't get something like this arranged in a few months."Nys said that the team isn't in danger of disappearing from the cyclo-cross peloton this season.He also denied that sports marketing and event company Golazo, which runs several cyclo-cross races and contributes to the team's youth structure and Sven Nys Academy, will step up to contribute to the senior squad."That is not true. We are part of 'the house', and they will of course continue to support us. But not in the way it is being suggested. No extra money will certainly need to be injected. In that respect, everything is covered for next year," he said."In the meantime, we have already found several additional shirt partners, who will be announced in the coming weeks. This means that we are already making concrete future plans."We are certainly not doomed. And we are diligently continuing our search... with the strong relationship with Golazo as a reliable foundation."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: What the Brazilian GP revealed about F1's ability to cope with rain
'I don't think I could do just one discipline' – How a mantra about circles, childhood friends and an unruly chicken help Puck Pieterse to do it all
item.author: Rosael Torres-Davis
item.content:encoded: Puck Pieterse folds a slice of pizza the way New Yorkers do, and her very first slice was plain cheese, nothing else. She doesn't usually order it that way, she told me later; she just wanted to taste the basic version first. That was lunch. For breakfast, she had a bagel with cream cheese and smoked salmon. Somewhere along the way, she hit the M&M's store in Times Square and went to town picking up every flavour she can't buy in the Netherlands. She ate enough that it made her feel sick. "It made me fly on the bike," she laughed. "I'm on holiday," she shrugged. Once her stomach settled, the leftovers became her post-ride recovery snack.It was 24-year-old Pieterse's first time in New York, and she told a small crowd of fans that evening that it was a lot to take in: the noise, the lights, the sheer scale of it. "It's just so much bigger than my European mind can comprehend," she said. She'd been to a Knicks game the night before. She was still processing the soundtrack: the organ, the sound effects narrating every possession, and an arena that left no doubt which side it was on, with ominous cues when the visitors had the ball and "crazy TikTok songs" when the Knicks did. You would never have guessed that from watching her ride on 8th Avenue at the start of rush hour earlier that day, or from how smoothly she handled clueless onlookers and city vehicles in a bustling Central Park just days before marathon weekend. Later that evening, at Roberta's Pizza in Midtown Manhattan, I had a little over 20 minutes and three slices of cake to win her trust. We were both speaking our second language, and we were both frazzled by the room, but the sweets helped break the ice. Pieterse rides for Fenix-Premier Tech, and everyone asks her the same question: how does she do it all? She races cyclo-cross in winter, the Classics in spring, and mountain bikes and the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift in summer, and she has won at the highest level in all three disciplines. "It's definitely getting harder to combine everything because every discipline is getting way more specific," she told me. Her 2026 season showed the cost: podiums at Flanders, Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Tour's polka-dot jersey and a third straight bronze at the cyclo-cross Worlds, but not the one standout victory she said she wanted.The more interesting question is how she keeps her head clear while doing it, how a rider pulled in so many directions stays steady in each one. She came to New York between the road and CX seasons, for a community ride and pizza night hosted by Canyon and Zwift, and I spent the day trying to find out to that question. The answer, it turned out, involved circles. And not just riding around in them.The question came from the crowd gathered on Roberta's rooftop, read aloud by the evening's host, Matt Stephens: did she have a mantra, or any trick for staying focused under pressure?She has circles, Pieterse explained. Circle one is the race and only the race: your line, your effort, what you are doing right now. Circle two sits a little wider; it can be your mom or dad shouting from the tape, and they are allowed in briefly, but then you go back to circle one. The danger is drifting further out. "On a bad day, you start hearing people talking about you, or your own head joins in with the negativity," she noted. She recognizes it happening and steps back inside.Her race mornings are built to keep the first circle uncluttered. At a cyclo-cross race, her father prepares her pre-race meal, she rides two or three laps of the course, then tries to visualize it back at the camper, with Dutch rap in her headphones. Nothing superstitious, she insisted. Back on 8th Avenue at peak time, circle one is a cab door, a delivery cyclist salmoning against the flow, a pedestrian stepping off the curb mid-text. Pieterse slid through the chaos without appearing to think. When I asked how she made urban survival look so effortless, she gave me a look that suggested it was not much of a question.To her, it is simply second nature. "If you race a lot, you get a bit of awareness about what others are going to do, but of course you can never be one hundred per cent sure," she said. At home in the Netherlands, she rides through a city centre every day to reach her group ride meeting point. Dutch cities are smaller, she notes, but there are more of them, so traffic is woven into every training ride. She knows her routes, including – she admits with a grin – when she might sneak through a red light."I think if you're less into cycling and you're a tourist here, it's really dangerous actually with all the cars."Still, she'd love to ride an alleycat race in New York, she said, before thinking better of it: it wouldn't be safe. NYC drivers, though, got a good review. "They know there are cyclists around, so that's nice."I watched most of it from a few bike lengths back, on a Canyon Aeroad borrowed from her sponsor. I chased her through Midtown and into Central Park, where about 40 riders had turned out for the Canyon and Zwift community ride, on a loop already crowded with marathon-weekend runners and visitors. Over three laps, Pieterse found her way to the wheel of nearly every rider, chatting and making jokes as she went.'Cross, Classics, and cakeMost fans on the ride wanted to know when her cyclo-cross season will start. Pieterse, who is still working out her 'cross schedule, was more curious about them: why they took up cycling in a city with so little room for it, and whether they only ride in the park or live somewhere with better roads. She was struck by how big the local community is, given how few bike shops she had spotted while walking around.I'd heard Pieterse plans rides around bakery stops, so she didn't argue when I told her we would do a cake tasting while we talked. Cakes and sweets are part of the programme. At her local coffee stop back home, she orders apple pie in slices so massive they are meant to be shared.She took the tasting seriously. The tiramisu was "surprisingly marshmallowy… when it should have been more mascarpone and alcohol," while the red velvet cake had the texture the tiramisu missed. "I know my cakes," she said. The key lime cake, airy and bright, ended up being her favourite.Between bites, I asked how she manages to switch between disciplines. She splits her year into blocks: road, mountain bike, with the Tour de France sandwiched in between, then back to the mountain bike. 'Cross fills the winter, and by January, she is deep into the intense CX calendar. By the end of February, she has pivoted back to the road for the Classics.The switch itself is smaller than people think, she insists. She trains on both bikes at home. She sees the Spring Classics and cross-country mountain biking as requiring the same type of explosive effort. The Classics are simply far longer, demanding deeper fatigue resistance.The hard part is accepting what she has to give up. Her Classics rivals spend an entire winter preparing only for those races, while she is racing 'cross. Before mountain bike Worlds, she notes, she could have been at an altitude camp instead of racing the Tour."I'm fully committed to cycling and to becoming the best cyclist I can be," she said. She accepts the trade-offs because variety gives her so much. Pressed by the crowd that night to choose just one discipline or bike, she called herself an all-rounder, then picked the mountain bike. "For now," she added. It circles back to her mental framework. The ground beneath her keeps changing, from mud to cobbles to singletrack, and her job is to keep circle one steady. Her record explains why people keep asking about her ability to do it all. In 2024, she won the elite cross-country mountain bike world title, then a stage of the Tour de France Femmes on her first attempt, along with the young rider's white jersey. In 2025, she won La Flèche Wallonne, then five MTB World Cup races in a row.Then came 2026. Before the Ardennes, she told her team she would "rather have one real stand-out result than three podiums." She got the podiums instead: third at Flanders, second at Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, no win.When asked which win she would relive, she chose the 2024 Tour stage from Valkenburg to Liège over the closing climbs of . That day, on rain-soaked roads, at just 22, she beat race leader Demi Vollering in a photo finish, with Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney third. "I had, in the evening before, in the night, I woke up... I dreamed that I was winning today," she told the room. "And then in the end, the final, I just knew what was going to happen. It was super weird."There is one major title still on her radar. She has stood on the elite cyclo-cross Worlds podium four years running, silver in 2023 and bronze in each of the three years since, but never on the top step. The next chance comes in Oostende, Belgium, at the end of January. A few moments after we talked about it, a stray balloon shaped like a number one drifted up over us and into the black-blue evening sky. 'It's sad that we don't have the US World Cups anymore'Pieterse knows North American 'cross better than most Europeans. She won the under-23 world title in Fayetteville, Arkansas, in 2022, and has raced World Cups in Iowa and Wisconsin. No World Cup has come back since the 2023/24 season. The 2026/27 series has 12 rounds, including Glasgow on December 13, but none in North America. When I told her that American cyclo-cross has struggled to regain its momentum in recent years, and asked what the US could learn from Europe, she was frank. "It's a very Belgian sport," she said. In Belgium, a fan can reach most races in about half an hour by car; here, she pointed out, it can take a seven-hour flight. What she liked about the American 'cross races she has done was the weekend format, with amateur and kids' races building to the World Cup on Sunday. She also wondered whether a late-season slot on the 'cross calendar might make the trip across the Atlantic easier on riders. Mountain biking, she noted, wrestles with the same question of where to put its World Cups."I think it's sad that we don't have the US World Cups anymore," she said. For riders, those races were a lot of fun, and though getting here is a long trip, "once you're here it's always been worth it." When the biggest names come, the public follows. Several people on the Central Park ride had told her they had watched her race 'cross here.The other fix, she thinks, is online. "I think being present on social media can play a big role as well," she said, though geo-restrictions make races harder to watch in the US. And 'cross suits a screen: at "only fifty minutes to an hour," she said, a CX race is easier to watch than a mountain bike race.Back to reality and racingWhilst New York is something of a holiday, her next big trips away will be for racing. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes starts in Leeds on July 30, the race's first Grand Départ in the UK. She missed the big-name climbs of recent editions and sees chances for herself and Fenix-Premier Tech on a route with shorter climbs. "I think it will only make maybe even a more exciting Tour."Home is Amersfoort, in the middle of the Netherlands, where she grew up and still lives. She started riding because her father came home muddy from weekend mountain bike rides with friends, and she wanted that too. As a kid, she said, announcing she would turn pro was like saying "you wanted to be a police officer or a firefighter," something you say without really meaning it. Then, as a first-year junior, she had a good enough season to earn a spot at the Worlds in cyclo-cross and mountain biking. By the time she was under-23 and had signed with Alpecin-Deceuninck, she was suddenly sharing a roster with Mathieu van der Poel.When things get heavy, she doesn't call cycling insiders. She calls a high school friend, a student whose life looks nothing like hers, whenever their schedules line up. And she calls Mischa Bredewold, who grew up two kilometres away. Bredewold is two years older and rode in the same club as Pieterse's sister, which made Puck the tag-along little sister for years. Now, both are professionals, and over the last couple of years they have grown close. Bredewold, Pieterse said, has a view on most things. "And it's usually a good opinion."New York is a city built on excess, and hers was a bag of M&M's. From there, she headed to a short team camp in Lisbon, with rides on city bikes, more pastries, and surfing lessons. Then it was back to the Netherlands, back to the mud, and back to Moncler, her pet chicken who terrorises the neighbourhood. "She attacks cats, ducks, dogs," Pieterse said. "Nothing is safe." That includes her mother."I don't think I could do just one discipline," she said. "I would go out of my mind." She needs the change of scenery, and believes the variety makes her "a more whole cyclist." After a day with her, I'd put it a little differently. The mud and the cobbles, the cakes, the surfboard, the friend who has nothing to do with bikes: none of it pulls her away from the racing. It's what keeps her whole enough to do it. Back to when the number-one balloon drifted above us, she didn't look up at it for long. A team camp was waiting, then a cyclo-cross season with the Worlds in Oostende at the end, and a rogue chicken at home in need of supervision. The city had been loud all day. As far as I could tell, circle one had stayed quiet.

item.title: F1's divisive wet weather tyres to change in 2027 - what needs solving
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 tyre supplier Pirelli is close to finalising new specification wet-weather tyres for next season that already address concerns drivers voiced last weekend. F1 had its first proper wet weekend of the year at Interlagos, with both qualifying and the race impacted by the rain.Saturday’s running took place in conditions that were so extreme that the wet tyre, which has rarely been used in recent years, became the preferred choice for the conditions.The race on Sunday was hit by showers, with drivers starting on intermediates, shifting to slicks and then reverting to inters towards the end when the rain returned.But despite there being no major incidents – and the race being the first this year not interrupted by either a virtual or full safety car – drivers were still unhappy with how the wet rubber behaved.Williams driver Carlos Sainz called for work to be done with Pirelli to deliver improvements in the future.“The level of the wet and the inter is not good enough and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre,” he said. “In the mixed conditions, the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear, by the time it warms up the front is gone.“And the extreme [wet], honestly, we had so much aquaplaning and a big lack of rear grip. So still missing a bit of development on these two tyres.” The biggest challenge that drivers faced with the intermediate tyre on Sunday was getting them up to operating temperature.This proved especially challenging on the low-speed laps to the grid, where a number of drivers were seen battling to keep their cars on the track.And things weren't much better in the race, as Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson said it had been a real challenge to get the tyres into the right operating window.The biggest problem was the temperature was much cooler,” Lawson said. “So even though there was less water on the laps of the grid, the cars were nearly undriveable. And the temps were just going down.“We survived the start of the race, but at points when it rains a lot, it's not that the standing water is too much; it's that you can't actually keep the temperature in it. So, if we're on a track like Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble.”But it was not just the fire-up that was a problem, as the inters proved very delicate in the race too.Alex Albon, who described the laps to the grid as “insane”, said things were not much better once the tyres were up to temperature.“It just feels like they never overheat or they never get up to temperature," he explained. "Then by the time you're circulating, the tread's already come off the tyre and then you're already struggling, you're sliding around.“So you never feel good at any point in the race; it never feels like it comes alive.”One of the common themes across this season is that the intermediate tyres feel worse than the previous version.Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who has long been sceptical about the inters ever since he tried them out at a wet test earlier this year, feels like they don't give as much confidence to push on as their predecessor.“Generally, I must say they feel very poor,” he said. “The grip, I don't know if it's only with our car, but compared to the inters we used to have in the previous years, it just feels like they're nowhere. Extremely poor grip.“The last stint felt [in Brazil] like I was driving on ice. So I want to review exactly what happened with our car. I don't know if it was the case for everyone, but it's genuinely not a very good tyre.”Gasly's point is well-founded because Pirelli has had to design a tyre for the 2026 rules that is theoretically a step away from what is ideal.The switch between straight mode and corner mode at the end of straights puts huge forces through the tyres, plus Pirelli needs to ensure its product can cope if active aero fails and cars are running down straights with maximum downforce.So in a similar vein to how straight mode consequences have forced increases in minimum slick tyre pressures, Pirelli had to make a more robust intermediate tyre.Furthermore, the minimum pressures have also gone up for wets and inters. In Brazil, for example, the minimum front pressures went up from 25.5psi last year on the inters to 28psi now, and on the wets from 22psi to 26.5psi.The impact is a tyre that does not move around as much - which does not inspire confidence from the drivers to lean on and is also much harder to warm up.The circumstances of the rule changes are something that Haas driver Ollie Bearman referenced in Brazil.“They are definitely a bit worse than last year’s ones,” he said. “There’s a few more parameters that the manufacturer has to put in mind when they design these tyres, because of the straight mode, ride heights and things like that.“The tyre feels a bit less forgiving: very stiff, very hard to warm up. Lap 1 was a big challenge. It’s a warm-up thing again for us, same as yesterday in quali.”And while drivers did manage to get through the Brazilian weekend, Interlagos has a rough track surface and a twisty infield section that helps put temperature into the rubber. That may not be true at all venues on the calendar.As Mercedes driver George Russell said: “I think it's important also to realise the three tracks driven on were very rough tarmacs and Malaysia was hot even in the rain.“Singapore sprint race was still hot and [Brazil qualifying], even though it was raining, it was 30 degrees and the track was 30 degrees. Maybe in 15 degrees of Spa, we're giving different feedback.”What Pirelli is looking to changePirelli always knew that it would need to fine-tune its wet tyres to the real 2026 cars, with the current designs having been based on feedback from mule car running last year.It had planned a wet test in Bahrain in February to help it work on understanding things better using an artificially soaked track, but that had to be abandoned in the wake of the Iran war beginning.Further wet weather tests over the season have been completed, which has put Pirelli on a path to introduce revised inters and wets for next season.While Pirelli motorsport boss Dario Marrafuschi does not want to reveal too many specifics about what is coming for 2027, he has confirmed that the warm-up issues on the inter will be addressed.“Tyre development is going ahead and we have a different spec for next year,” he told The Race."Some of the drivers were complaining about warm-up, so we have been working for next year on the warm-up phase, on the intermediates.”He added: “It doesn't mean we are not satisfied with this year's specs because we had very good racing in Malaysia, in Singapore and in Brazil as well. But an optimisation can be done.“We always listen quite openly to the comments of the drivers."The final homologation of the wet and inter tyre designs with the FIA will be made in December, when more details will be revealed about what is changing for next year.But Marrafuschi also believes there is an element that, in the meantime, teams will get a better handle on how to get more from the inter now that they have some proper experience of it.He thinks what was highlighted in Brazil was how some squads and drivers seem to have had a better understanding of what was needed than others.“Clearly there are some cars or drivers, some set-ups or whatever, that are more comfortable in one condition or the other," he explained.“We saw in the beginning of the race, Lewis [Hamilton] having an astonishing performance, with zero warm-up problems at all. "We know that other drivers, since the formation laps, were complaining about the front-end warm-up. So, there are some tunings that are in the hands of the teams.”

item.title: Past results and wildcard invitations now define 'pro' categories at The Traka World Series events, The Rift keeps a limited number of entries open for women - Gravel Bits
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Organisers of The Traka World Series, formerly Gravel Earth Series, announced the ranking procedures to determine overall winners for 2027, with balanced points for the top 25 riders in pro divisions at each of the seven races, and a new system for riders to earn entry into the pro category as well.There will be no enhanced scores for individual events, which had been the case in the past at The Traka 360 and the series finale, The River. At Traka Girona and the final series stop, now The Last Dance, points will be the same as other events. In the past, riders could compete at either The Traka 200 or The Traka 360, or both, which was rare, with more points on the line in the longer distance. This year, pro fields will be consolidated in the reworked 300km distance on May 1, which will offer points and recognise clear winners in the big tune-up before Unbound Gravel. There are new criteria for riders to line up in the pro division for the popular Girona race, which prioritise results from last year. Riders having finished within 5% of the winning time in their gender category can race as pros. Top finish times from the year before also apply from The Traka 200, Santa Vall, and the longer distances from Ranxo Gravel, Gravel Desert and The River 160. And at the first three series races in 2027, the same 5% margin will apply for riders to gain pro status, including a new event in late spring referred to as 'The Traka in the Americas'. Organisers added that a limited number of wild card entries would be considered, "assessed on the sporting information provided and the eligibility criteria of each application".There will be no minimum number of events required in the series, however, athletes must start the season finale in October, The Last Dance. Once the seventh and final event has been completed, the final standings will be decided from points earned after dropping the two lowest scores in the calendar. The final top 10 in The Traka World Series pro leaderboards, men and women, will share a €20,000 overall prize purse. At each event, the top five pro riders, men and women, will have another €8,000 on offer, with CORE4's purse double that amount.The Rift gravel race in Iceland is officially sold out for 2027, but organisers announced a few days ago that they are keeping a limited number of entries open for women in the 200-kilometre distance. They want 200 women on the July 24 start line for the 200km distance.Started in 2019, The Rift offers routes from 60km to 330km from Hvolsvöllur, Iceland across the rough volcanic highlands, marked by multiple icy-cold water crossings. The 200km distance is considered the main event, won last year by Anton Stensby and Haley Smith.Registration for The Rift 200k is $320. For any rider, male or female, who wishes to compete in shorter categories - 140km or 60km - opportunities are still available to join the waitlist. The long-distance 'Abyss' event is closed.Valley of Tears returns next year for a fourth year, March 5-6, with two days of racing in Turkey, Texas. Organisers announced they will expand the number of titles on offer for the USA Cycling Collegiate Gravel National Championships, with four stars-and-stripes jerseys up for grabs in 2027.A star-studded elite field is expected to compete for a $45,000 prize purse, split evenly between pro women and pro men. The first payouts are at Friday's Dirt Crit presented by QTS with $10,000 for pro/open competitors. The balance is shared on Saturday for the 93-mile main event, with chunky gravel, old rail trail, sand and singletrack that passes through Caprock Canyons State Park.In 2026, Valley of Tears hosted the inaugural nationals for collegiate riders, won by Nate Meister (Fort Lewis) and Emma Kasza-James (Midwestern State). Fort Lewis College took the team title. This year, four categories will be offered - Varsity Men, Varsity Women, Club Men and Club Women.The event offers three ride distances - 20 miles, 50 miles and 93 miles. Registration is limited to 1,000 riders across all fields and opens with discounted rates at 7:00 a.m. CDT on December 1, 2026.Last year, Sofia Gomez Villafane (Specialized Off-road) captured her third consecutive victory at Valley of Tears, holding off Paige Onweller (Trek Driftless), while Alexey Vermeulen (ENVE) won from a three-rider sprint among the elite men.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Liberty Media founder sells voting power of F1's parent company
item.author: Samarth Kanal
item.content:encoded: Liberty Media founder and ex-chairman John Malone has sold his significant voting power in Formula 1's parent company.Malone founded Liberty Media in 1991 and stepped down as chairman of the board in 2026, nine years after Liberty Media acquired F1 for $4.6billion USD (£3.4bn).Malone was the most significant voting shareholder of Liberty Media until early November 2026 when Liberty Media announced that it had purchased Malone's 'high-vote' stock and exchanged it for 'low-vote' stock, essentially diluting Malone's voting power from around 48% to 3%.Liberty Media purchased the high-vote stock after Malone received "a number of unsolicited offers from third parties" to acquire it.The transaction effectively eliminates the transfer of Malone's voting power to a third party and strengthens Liberty Media shareholders' power in voting matters - such as a sale of F1.In 2025, Malone said on the Opening Bid Unfiltered finance podcast that Liberty would be open to a sale of F1 - with the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) among F1's then-touted suitors.He said F1 "has an exceptionally good economic structure", adding: "It's a public company. If somebody gets carried away, and they want to buy it, and they're willing to pay more for it than the board thinks that they can deliver to the shareholders, then we would sell it. That's the bottom line."Liberty Media president and CEO Derek Chang said during the company's Q3 earnings call that Malone "controlled a significant set of votes with a relatively low economic interest".He explained that Liberty Media's purchase of the voting shares "helps us effectively control our own destiny forward".There is no indication that Liberty Media is considering a sale of F1 in 2026.Chang added: "We're still focused primarily on growing the businesses that we have. And as we stated previously, sort of investing behind those businesses and growth plans that they have is probably the biggest priority as we think about other forms of capital allocation."The net worth of F1 sits at nearly $28bn as of November 2026, with the average value of an F1 team having reached $3.6bn in 2025 according to Forbes.In 2025, Liberty Media completed its acquisition of an 84% stake in MotoGP commercial rights holder Dorna for around $3.3bn or €3.02bn.

item.title: Canyon-SRAM delve into world of AI with new training and development partnership ahead of 2027 season
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Canyon-SRAM have announced an AI research and development partner for the remainder of 2026, with the German squad working with FasCat Coaching as they prepare for the 2027 season.In what looks to be a first in the women's peloton, Canyon-SRAM will use FasCat's CoachCat AI coaching platform to run an "AI-powered season review" on their riders to help prepare for the new season.The team say that CoachCat can analyse riders' performance history throughout their career "to identify patterns and insights that might otherwise go unnoticed." The system is said to be capable of examining the effectiveness of training blocks based on several metrics, including heat, altitude, training load, heart rate, and sleep monitoring.Canyon-SRAM worked with FasCat in the lead-up to this year's Tour de France Femmes, with the company analysing their riders' historical data to generate predictions for the race itself and training and preparation beyond."WorldTour teams are sitting on a wealth of untapped data that could tell them exactly why a rider won or lost, and what to change. CoachCat finds that in minutes, not months. Working with Canyon-SRAM lets us prove at the highest level of the sport what our AI does every day for the athletes on our platform," said Frank Overton, founder and CEO of FasCat coaching, which has been in business since 2003.Lucinda Brand, Steffi Häberlin, and Georgia Baker lead the incoming list, while young German talent Antonia Niedermaier will take Niewiadoma-Phinney's leadership role at the year's biggest races."We are always looking for new ways to understand performance, and AI analysis of a rider’s full history is a natural next step," said Canyon-SRAM performance director Dan Fleeman."FasCat’s AI analytics give our performance staff a fresh, objective look at what has driven each rider’s best results and where we can build for 2027. We have enjoyed exploring this together.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Rossi in new autobiography: '2015 still hurts, Marquez wanted me to lose'
You asked, we answered: Our Labs experts on wind tunnel testing, reverse mullet wheels, our ultimate Roubaix setups and more – AskCN
item.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
item.content:encoded: Welcome to the first edition of Ask CN, a new AMA-style series on where our readers get the chance to put their questions to us, our columnists, and more. For the inaugural episode, we're shining a light on CN Labs, the longstanding series of wind tunnel tests, rolling resistance tests and other empirical inquisitions into bikes, gear and industry trends.Over the course of the past week, subscribers, readers and followers have been submitting questions to Josh, Will and Tom - the CN tech team responsible for the aforementioned tests. Today, subscribers alone will get to read their answers. So whether you're curious about the technical details of our wind tunnel protocol, want to know what future tests we have in mind, or even the bike we'd choose for Roubaix, you'll find it below. And if you're not yet subscribed, then there's no better time to join our ever-growing community that gets unlimited access to all our industry-leading tests, expert tech insight, comprehensive race coverage, and plenty of subscriber-exclusive articles, like our AskCN Q&As! Do you have a standard setup or a standard bike on which you calibrate your equipment in order to make sure you can compare results from different campaigns? (Kleinkaro)Start with an easy one… we do! We have my old Trek Emonda ALR, a bike that I bought in around 2016 when I worked at a bike shop. It spent a couple of years untouched in my garage and was eventually donated to the CN Labs cause in 2024. Nowadays it lives in the office store and remains unchanged between tests so that we can use it as a 'baseline' to compare against every time we test other bikes. I trusted this was a solid theory, but we verified it in 2025 when we did our 12 aero bikes test. We not only took along the Emonda, but also the Scott Foil we'd also tested in 2024 as a second 'baseline'. Using the same protocols, both bikes were around six watts faster than the previous year. If we didn't take a baseline at all, we'd have just concluded that everything tested in 2025 was a similar amount (six watts) faster than the bikes we tested in 2024, even if they were actually equivalent. The difference between the two baselines (the Foil was around 35 watts faster) changed by just 0.65w across the two tests. Do we know how much difference modern aero clothing (aero fabrics, speed suits, aero socks etc..) makes to rider speed/power compared to the rather looser, less technical fabrics of clothing from (even the not-so-distant) past? (Bernard the Badger)The big caveat is that clothing is massively rider dependent, so the actual savings are to be taken with a pinch of salt, but in 2025, we got hold of an outfit at each price point from Kalas, and tested how they varied. We had the entry-level bibs and jersey, the next tier up, a road skinsuit, a time trial skinsuit, and a double-layered super-suit designed for Olympic athletes. We also threw in some extra aero accessories too. We found 18 watts between the fastest and slowest options, but perhaps most interesting was that there was as much variance between the different high end options as there was between cheap and expensive. This, we believe, is because when you get into the high-end options, fabric choice is tailored to speed.When will you test the new Orca Aero and SL9? Also, any plans to test TT bikes too? Or skinsuits? (flowerforalgernon)Both of those bikes are conversations in progress. I have an SL9 here for review, but it's not in the correct size for fair wind tunnel testing. As for TT bikes, it's not something we've got in the pipeline for now, but it's not off the table for next year. Skinsuits, aside from testing the difference across price points mentioned above, we've not done a skinsuit head-to-head because the results are so rider-, position-, and speed-dependent. We'd either need to do it as a bit of fun, knowing the results aren't super helpful to our readers, or do it using multiple different riders, of different genders and sizes, across a load of different speeds. That's probably more than a single day in the tunnel, which isn't a dealbreaker, but I think there are higher-priority tests that we should do first. I’d really like to know the aero impacts of a mullet setup, like the Factor Elara, 64 up front and 46 in the rear. Does that combo give the best aero and weight setup? I currently run a Zipp XPLR up front and a 650b in the rear on my Cannondale Topstone gravel setup for tyre clearance, but I don’t notice any aero penalty with the 650b in the rear. Does the wind tunnel have anything to say? (Nathan W Ramsey, via email)You won't believe me, but we planned to do this before aero mullets were cool.Back in 2024, when we ran our second (of three so far) aero road wheel group test, we took along some Zipp 808s and 404s. We planned to test them as sold, then run some mullet / reverse mullet tests. Sadly, we ran out of time that day and haven't come back to the idea since. I'll definitely add this idea back onto the list, though.For some added context, the closest we've come to your setup is running different tyre widths front and rear. Interestingly, a 38mm front with 2.0 rear is 1.1% slower than a 2.0 front and 38mm rear (on 700c Hunt CGR40 wheels, tested as a bike only using an Allied Able frame). This was done in connection with our gravel tyre width test. Would love to see a tunnel review of the Cervélo Aspero-5, which is curiously missing from the stable of gravel bikes tested (toadpalmer)We tried for our gravel bike shoot out back in May. Cervélo promised a bike, but then went quiet on us, and it never showed. I think our contact at PON was juggling a few Cannondale-related things at the time, but it's definitely on the radar for the future. The Áspero-5 is a different beast from bikes like the Crux and the Elara though, which each offer 10mm+ more tyre clearance, so that should factor into buying decisions. How about a handlebar showdown? As this is a leading edge, what about exposed cables versus internal routing for the same bars / one piece vs. aero bar and stem etc. It seems like this could be a good place to find some speed without changing one's whole bike (older frames unite LOL) (btlrck)Can you test against a pre-aero bike from around 2016? E.g. Focus Izalco Max, then ridden by Team AG2R. Some of us are stuck with bikes from that era. I am doing some early research on a new race bike, so I'd like to know how much I am gaining with a new aero bike both on the flat and on climbs. And please always include the weight of the bikes, including the pedals. Thanks. (brookelazich)I've combined these two questions because my answer to both leads down a similar path...On the handlebar suggestion, I've steered clear so far because new bikes are invariably sold with proprietary one-piece cockpits, and so fewer and fewer new bikes are customisable in this way. However, I do appreciate that it ignores not only older frames, but the more budget end of the spectrum too. As for the suggestion of testing a couple of older race bikes as a means to benchmark their performance in the wider standings, this is something I'm keen to try to make happen in 2027.And to combine the answers into one thread, what could work well is taking a couple of old bikes. Focus Izalco Max, SuperSix Evo 3, Venge Vias(!?), and seeing how much we can close the gap to a modern bike. This probably won't happen very quickly, because we have a few other big projects in early 2027 to focus on (more on this soon), but it's on the list. As for the pedals, we weigh without, as we don't know whether our readers are using Shimano, Look, Speedplay etc. Would a 35mm tyre fitted to a rim optimised for 35mm tyres be as aero as a 28mm tyre on a rim optimised for 28mm tyres? (tc_fair_weather_rides)Why are wider tyres more aerodynamic? (Cycle Tech Ireland)Another duo of questions combined here, as they sort of ask the same thing. To answer the first question: in our testing, they're not. They might be faster, but with everything else kept equal, they're slower. To answer the second: it's a simple no when querying aero alone, but complicated when you try to solve for speed. With all else equal, a narrower 28mm setup will be more aerodynamic when both are optimised for their respective tyre widths. A bigger tyre on a bigger rim has a larger frontal area – the A in the CdA equation. To give some data to answer this, here's a graph. As tyre width grows, so does aero drag. A 32mm tyre on the Zipp 303 XPLR wheel is faster than a 28mm tyre on the Hunt CGR 40, but this will mostly be because the Zipp wheel is 14mm deeper.Remember, though, speed isn't only made up of aerodynamics. I implore you to read our test on 40mm tyres, as we tackled this question fairly head-on. On rougher surfaces, a 35mm tyre is 13 watts faster (per tyre) than a 28mm tyre. When we swapped to a different rim optimised for wider tyres, that saving grew to around 55w per tyre. However, on smooth tarmac, the benefit of going wider was actually negative. Rolling resistance didn't change with any significance, and the aero got marginally worse. So the real trade-off is aero versus rolling resistance on the surface you ride, plus a little bit of weight, cornering and acceleration peppered into the equation too. And you'll probably find that the lower tyre pressure of wider tyres means more comfort, better grip, and less chance of a puncture too.In your wind tunnel tests, why do you take the seven different angles in such a narrow band? Why not 45 degrees, or at least 30 degrees, along with straight, 10, 20...? (Kelly Wilde)This is down to what yaw angles you're actually likely to experience when riding. Since there isn't one predominant wind direction the world over (i.e., it blows in all directions, and we travel in all directions), we can agree that the most common wind you'll face when cycling is the air that you ride through, equivalent, therefore, to the speed you travel. And since you always travel forwards on a bike, if there were no ambient wind at all, you'd experience a 0° yaw (as is common in a velodrome). But even if the wind is coming at you from 90° to the right, the actual experienced yaw angle will be less than this, because you're creating your own headwind by moving through air. There are a few mathematical models that have calculated - in extreme detail - the likelihood of experiencing any given wind angle at any given time, taking into account ambient wind conditions, average riding speeds and so on. To solve for watts, we calculate a weighted average based on the weightings supplied by one of these mathematical models.The models all create a bell curve that centres around 0°, and in all cases, the probability of experiencing anything beyond 15° on either side is so small that it doesn't make any difference to the results when we calculate that average, and thus it would be a waste of time to test it.Now that you know all the data on rolling resistance and aero, what would you spec as the ultimate Roubaix bike for a normal rider? (itcanalwaysbelouder)This one felt like a good question to pose to the whole team, so you'll find individualised responses below, starting with Tom Wieckowski, who rode the Roubaix Sportive in 2024. Next up is Will Jones, who has fronted the Cyclingnews Tech YouTube channel since its launch in Spring, during which time he's ridden and reviewed over two dozen flagship race bikes.And finally, me (Josh Croxton).What's more aero: Moustache or clean-shaven? (Will Strickson)To wrap up with a silly one... this question comes from Will Strickson, the Web Editor over at our most hated mortal enemies at Cyclist Magazine. We all know hair is the enemy of aero, so the initial theory is that clean-shaven wins out. However, trip strips have proven effective in clothing, so would they not apply here too? Alex Dowsett once shaved trip strips into his leg hair, so in 2027, we're going to make Will Jones grow just the vertical segments of a handlebar 'tache and see whether the aero savings outweigh the friends he loses along the way. That's all for today, folks. With so many questions still to answer, I've convinced my colleagues to let me do a second part in the coming weeks. Feel free to drop any new questions into the comments of this article, and I'll endeavour to get to them. And with that, thanks for reading!

item.title: FIA reveals ADUO results in final review of 2026 F1 season
Hand injury from crash on way to Euros bronze forces Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado out of upcoming cyclo-cross races
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: A late crash during Saturday’s UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships not only prevented Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado from fighting for the win, but has forced the Fenix-Premier Tech rider out of this week's racing.Alvarado had been in a with a shout of winning the elite women’s race in Zeddam on Saturday, but was gapped on the final ascent of the punishing 99-step run up. Then, while battling to return to the leading duo of Marie Schreiber and Lucinda Brand, she crashed, injuring her hand.After the crash Alvarado could be seen shaking the injured hand, and by the time she crossed the line in third place, she was unable to hold the handlebars.Medical examinations since the incident have revealed Alvarado had sustained a ligament tear to her right thumb, and a date for her return to competition is uncertain."She will wear a custom-made brace, and her return to cyclocross racing will depend on how her recovery progresses. We wish her a speedy recovery!" read a post on both Alvarado's and her team's Instagram account.Alvarado had been scheduled to race this Wednesday, November 11, at the third round of the Superprestige at Niel, but that is now out of the question, with this weekend’s Merksplas round and the X2O Trofee race at Hamme-Zogge also looking unlikely.With Alvarado out of contention following her crash, the race was notable for the controversial relegation of Luxembourgish rider Marie Schreiber. Though she crossed the line in first place, the victory was awarded to Brand after Schreiber's sprint was judged as irregular, the 23-year-old later accusing the commissaires of stealing the biggest moment of her career.Alvarado is one of the sport’s leading lights and has won almost every honour in the sport. She is the current Dutch national champion and won both the World and European Championships in 2020, as well as the season-long World Cup in 2024. She is yet to hit the heights this season, though her third place at the Euros was an indication she was progressing towards her best form.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Tour Down Under announces former Giro winner Jai Hindley as first headline starter for 2027
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: There are just 70 days to go until WorldTour racing resumes at the Tour Down Under in Australia, but as the anticipation builds for the 2027 season, the first big-name rider on the start list has already been announced: former Giro d'Italia winner Jai Hindley.It will mark 10 years since he made his debut riding for the national team UniSA-Australia at the Tour Down Under, and will be his first start since 2023. Despite his GC talents, Hindley has never won his home race, with overall results of 16th, 18th, 18th, and 25th from his four appearances, also taking the start in 2019 and 2020.The 30-year-old will lead Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in South Australia, having extended his contract with the German team through 2028 back in July. Also already confirmed alongside him will be New Zealand teammate Laurence Pithie, a former Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race winner making his fifth appearance in a row. "I haven’t raced the Tour Down Under since 2023, so I’m really looking forward to returning," said Hindley. "It’s a great way to kick off the season, racing in the Australian summer and on home roads in front of the Aussie fans."The support for the Australian riders is always fantastic, and there’s such a great atmosphere around the race. It’s always a fun event to be part of, and I’m excited to get the 2027 season under way with what I’m sure will be a strong team."Racing at the men's Tour Down Under will kick off on January 19 in Henley Beach, with six days of action via the Mount Lofty, Corkscrew Road, and Willunga Hill climbs set to decide the next Ochre jersey. If Vine returns to defend the jersey, he will be one of the heavy favourites alongside Hindley. Despite his lack of a GC win or podium in the TDU, the latter had a stellar 2026 season for Red Bull, riding to a third-place finish overall at the Giro d'Italia, and taking 15th on GC at the Tour de France while supporting overall runner-up Remco Evenepoel. "We are thrilled to welcome Jai back to the Santos Tour Down Under and I’m sure all cycling fans will be excited to watch him in action on South Australian roads," said race director Stuart O'Grady. "He holds a significant place in Australian cycling history as a Grand Tour winner, and at the age of 30 he remains in the prime of his career so we are getting to see the best of him. The course suits his characteristics with his all-round ability complemented nicely by his ability to climb with the best in the peloton."I’m sure Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe will again field a strong team to open the UCI WorldTour season, and having Jai here along with New Zealander Laurence Pithie brings some real quality to the peloton."It will be a history-making edition of the Tour Down Under, as the first-ever WorldTour race to hold men’s and women’s racing over the same distance on the same days. After the first three days of action in the men's event, the women's will run concurrently from January 22-24 across three identical routes from Glenelg to Victor Harbor, Christies Beach to Willunga Hill, and Norwood to Stirling.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
