item.title: TotalEnergies becomes XEFI as new title sponsor steps in to save French team
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The future of Jean-René Bernaudeau’s historic French team is secure, with the outfit currently known as TotalEnergies unveiling a new title sponsor in the form of XEFI, a French IT firm. The team, which started out as the Vendée youth squad in 1991, has been in the professional peloton since 2000, with the likes of Thomas Voeckler and Pierre Rolland making their mark on the Tour de France over the years, but the threat of its disappearance has loomed large all season. However, on November 9, three weeks after the initial deadline for UCI licence applications, the team announced a new sponsorship agreement with XEFI, on a three-year agreement. From 2027, the team will simply be named XEFI. "I am particularly delighted to see XEFI join forces with Vendée Cyclisme, a company with which we share much more than ambition: a genuine vision of people and the future," said Bernaudeau."Personal fulfilment, kindness, high standards, dedication to a job well done and training are at the heart of our shared values."XEFI is a French company based in Lyon that provides ‘a complete and integrated suite of IT services’ to some 25,000 small and medium-sized businesses. The firm has been involved with cycling before as a sponsor of the VC Villefranche-Beaujolais amateur team in France. "I never thought one day we’d have a partner that resembles us this much," said Bernaudeau in a video message that preceded the announcement. The announcement went on to liken the team’s development pathway – which includes its sports-study program for juniors (CREF) and its Vendée U development squad – with XEFI’s training apprenticeship schemes. It also detailed XEFI’s commitment to sport, through the VC Villefranche-Beaujolais team and the company’s employee sports-health program. "This project is not about blindly pushing forward, but about restoring meaning to elite sport while remaining true to our beliefs and our commitment to transparency," said Bernaudeau. "We firmly believe that success begins with developing and supporting the women and men of tomorrow. Since the creation of CREF in 1991, followed by Vendée U – Primeo Energie, our ambition has remained unchanged: to give young people from our region the same opportunities that I was fortunate enough to have. To develop athletes, but above all, to help shape individuals,""Selflessness, courage and solidarity are values we have always stood for. This partnership with XEFI allows us to uphold these values and take them to a new level through a medium-term project that we are all incredibly excited about."Where does this leave the team? The financial value of XEFI’s three-year sponsorship was not disclosed, so it is not clear how the team’s budget will compare to the years of TotalEnergies’ title sponsorship. However, the team appear confident of continuing along their current tracks, even if they have lost a number of their best riders amid the uncertainty surrounding the team’s future. The team currently operates as a second-division ProTeam and that is expected to be the case again once the team is now able to submit its finalised paperwork for 2027 to the UCI. TotalEnergies were the fourth-ranked ProTeam in 2026, meaning they missed out on automatic invitations to the Grand Tours but do get to race all the one-day events in the WorldTour calendar. They are also eligible for wildcard invitations so will be hopeful of securing a 28th consecutive appearance at the Tour de France. The team’s top-ranked rider in 2026, Jordan Jegat, has left for Lidl-Trek, though a big move for the Frenchman was always likely regardless of the team’s troubles. Classics specialist Anthony Turgis and Nicolas Breuillard are off to XDS Astana, while Alexandre Delettre, Sandy Dujardin, and Emilien Jeannière are off to the French WorldTour team Groupama-FDJ United. Meanwhile, Pierre Thierry is off to the French ProTeam Cofidis, while Mathieu Burgaudeau, Thomas Bonnet and Mattéo Vercher have all moved to fellow second-division outfits.Several riders have not inked contracts elsewhere and are expected to re-sign but in any case the team still has a long way to go in filling out a roster for 2027. On Monday, it was announced that the former Tour de France yellow jersey wearer Tony Gallopin will join as a sports director. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: From Lorena Wiebes to Paul Magnier – Who were the best sprinters of 2026?
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Surely we all love a bunch kick? The tension, the uncertainty, the chaos and the sheer speed, the strutting arms-in-the-air celebrations and the bar-banging of the losers can make hours watching an otherwise mundane day of a stage race all worthwhile. While there might be only a small group of riders able to win at the highest level, it’s the most highly competitive area of the sport, even when there are only a couple of the best sprinters in the final, you can bet your bottom dollar there’ll be plenty of pretenders trying their luck.And while sheer power is, of course, vital, winning isn’t all about legs, reading the ebb and flow of a fast moving group is essential, and timing is equally important, using whatever slipstream there is before emerging into the wind at the perfect moment to ensure your maximum effort counts.Then there’s the lead-out, making the high speed chaos all around slow down so the right decisions are made at the right time. And the best sprinters can either profit off their teammates’ work or surf the wheels to be in the right place at the right time. Sprinting is a true art. But who were the best artists in 2026? Among the women, there can be only one dominant rider, but on the men’s side it’s much harder to determine who was best. When the sprinter’s job is to finish the job of the team and win, statistics count for everything, so we've ranked seven of the best by their wins. Lorena Wiebes set out her stall for the year in February, dominating the UAE Tour Women and winning all three flat stages for the second consecutive season. She wore the yellow jersey after winning the opening two stages at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift and won two general classifications, at the Tour de Pologne and Tour of Chongming Island, where she won all the stages.Winning from February through to October, she showed remarkable resilience, though there were some interesting blips. At the Ronde van Brugge she lost the record which had seen her win every bunch sprint she’d contested since the 2024 Tour de France Femmes, finishing ninth behind Carys Lloyd (Movistar). Worse, though, was her disqualification when commissaires found her bike to be underweight after she won the opening stage of the Giro d’Italia.Despite a crash during the Track World Championships, where she won the Scratch Race rainbow jersey, she’ll be back and looking for retribution next year, and no one would be surprised if she adds another 24 victories to her total.Having turned professional as recently as 2024, Paul Magnier is rapidly blossoming into the sprinter to beat in the men’s peloton. He won his first professional race, bagging a further four victories that year, before taking a whopping 19 wins in his second season.That number might have dipped to 15 in 2026, but he equalled his tally of six WorldTour wins, and the total is still formidable, especially when considering he shares the team’s WorldTour sprinting duties with Tim Merlier.At this year’s Giro d’Italia the 22-year-old Frenchman showed remarkable progression, delivering a hugely contrasting performance to last year’s first participation, when he managed only three top-10 placings and failed to finish. This time round he won three stages and wore the cyclamen jersey for all but two days, eventually taking home his first Grand Tour points classification. As for his other victories, they came in a steady flow throughout the year, proving not only his consistency, but his place at the forefront of an emerging breed of sprinters, who are arguably more able to win after a lumpy day than their predecessors. That Soudal-QuickStep have two sprinters in our list is an indication of the team’s pivot away from targeting general classifications to stages and Classics. With Tim Merlier they had someone ready made to take advantage, and while he was behind teammate Paul Magnier in the list of overall winners for the season, 14 victories is a great haul.While Magnier is the young pretender, Merlier is the wily old timer, and though he may not be as versatile as the French tyro, he knows his way around a bunch kick better than most, and is able to deploy a prolonged burst of power few others can match. This means he is often able to rescue lost causes, and makes him perfect for the chaos of high-stakes Grand Tour sprints. At the Tour de France this year Merlier equalled the previous best ever Grand Tour return set at the 2024 Giro d’Italia, taking three stages before abandoning on stage 15. That took his tally of Tour stage wins to six, winning at least one in each of his three participations at the world’s biggest race. However, though those victories count for a lot, those were his only WorldTour wins of the year, with the bulk of his 14 successes coming at second tier .Pro level.This is, perhaps, an indication that the team’s sprinting mantel is gradually being handed from the 33-year-old to Magnier, though the older man is sure to fight to keep hold of his status as their leading sprinter.If Matthew Brennan hadn’t established himself as one of the peloton’s best sprinters by winning 12 races last season, his first as a professional, he certainly did in 2026. Not only did he match that total, but the 21-year-old stamped his authority on his first Grand Tour by winning five stages. And there might have been more had Wout van Aert, Visma-Lease a Bike’s star name, not been in the race, the team diverting some of their efforts to the Belgian’s successful pursuit of the points jersey.Brennan’s Vuelta performance, and two earlier wins at the Vuelta a Burgos, not only helped to establish himself as a top contender, but kickstarted his season after a barren period. Between March and September last year he won in all but one month, while this year seemed less consistent, success coming in clusters.Still only 20, he began 2026 winning a stage of the Santos Tour Down Under and finishing second three times. Back in Europe he bagged a maiden Classics victory at Kuurne-Brussel-Kuurne, but in the following five months he only cracked the top 10 four times, though three of those were stage wins at the third tier Flèche du Sud.Such blips are a sprinter’s lot, though, especially one so young, and we can expect more from Brennan in 2027.Despite winning more in 2026 than in any of his previous seasons, Jonathan Milan’s slightly under-par Giro d’Italia and non-attendance at the Tour de France meant he flew slightly under the radar in 2026. Half of his 12 wins came early in the year, but illness and injury left him short of form and rhythm in the middle part of the year. The 26-year-old started his season perfectly with victory at the opening two stages of the AlUla Tour, following that with three more wins at the UAE Tour. However, things started to go awry back in Europe, and though he won the final stage at Tirreno-Adriatico, illness ruined the rest of his spring. He arrived at the Giro d’Italia having not raced for almost a month, and coming up against an in-form Paul Magnier, his chances of a third maglia ciclamino were soon gone. Though he managed three top five finishes, he had to wait until the final day in Rome to claim a victory, second place in the points classification scant consolation. He gained some momentum during the summer, though, after winning his first Italian road title, Milan beat Magnier into second on two of his three stage wins at the Tour de Pologne. Then victory at stage 1 of the Renewi Tour was perhaps a highlight, beating the likes of Merlier, Olav Kooij, Jasper Philipsen and other sprinting royalty, but his season was over two days later when he crashed out.While he took more wins than ever, without bad luck, 2026 might have been an even better year for Milan.Elisa Balsamo might not have been able to best Wiebes during the 2026 season, indeed, she’s not won a race ahead of the Dutch rider since 2023, but 2026 saw the former World Champion return to somewhere near her best form, winning more WorldTour races than any year since 2022. Winning six times through the season, Balsamo took the bulk of her team’s victories, and while she might not have been so prolific had Wiebes not been forced out of the Giro d’Italia Women, she held the overall lead for three days, winning four stages of her home Grand Tour and taking the overall points classification. Another standout feature of Balsamo’s 2026 successes were their quality, with all but one of her six victories coming at WorldTour level, while at the other, the 1.1 level Egmont Cycling Race, her sprint was so powerful she put three seconds into second place.One win which showed Balsamo’ versatility was at the Classic Lorient Agglomération, a race rarely won by a pure sprinter and better suited to Classics specialists, setting her apart from Wiebes, who has never started in Plouay.For the first time in a while Charlotte Kool seemed to be returning to somewhere close to her best during 2026, last season’s mid-season move to Fenix-Premier Tech finally bearing fruit. With six wins, it was her best year since 2023, her first season as a lead sprinter. However, in contrast to that year, none of her six wins during 2026 came at WorldTour level, with two 1.Pro victories her best return.While she failed to trouble the scorers at the UAE Tour, Kool’s spring campaign was excellent, taking four wins between March 1 and mid-May, and finishing outside the top 10 only twice in 12 starts. But as the season wore on her form tailed off, failing to finish either the Giro d’Italia Women or the Tour de France Femmes, though she managed a stage win at the Baloise Ladies Tour, a race where she’s won seven stages earlier in her career.Kool is a class act, but, like every other sprinter in the women’s bunch, she’s found beating Lorena Wiebes all but impossible. However, she has beaten her in the years since the two were teammates at DSM in 2022, most notably and recently at the 2024 Tour de France, and if she can find her best form and some confidence, she may well do so again in 2027.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir
item.author: Niha Masih
item.content:encoded: From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolutionFew love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)Continue reading...

item.title: 'My lifelong dream has come true' - Rising gravel stars carve close victories at Iceman Cometh against former winners Alexey Vermeulen, Deanna Mayles
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Up-and-coming gravel racers Samanth Johnson, 22, and Kyan Olshove, 24, powered to elite titles at Iceman Cometh Challenge on Saturday, both holding off past champions in sprint finishes. Olshove claimed the top step of his home race on his sixth attempt. The Traverse City native was overcome at the finish, posting 1:32:57 after 31 miles, which was one second faster than his Michigan rival, Alexey Vermeulen."Still can't believe this is real… Thank you to everyone who made it possible. My life long dream has come true. It means everything to me," Olshove, who debuted this year in the Life Time Grand Prix, posted to Instagram.Vermeulen has won the Michigan race three times, most recently in 2023 when he held off 10 riders in a final sprint, including Olshove, who was third. From a long line of chasers this time, Mika Comaniuk of Quebec out-sprinted Alexander Woodford of Ontario for third.The route follows forested dirt roads, singletrack, doubletrack, and abandoned railroad lines, using the Vasa trail system, and the race changes the route each year. Sharp hills are prevalent in the final miles, and this time the 700-yard (1km) climb of Icebreaker hill was replaced with the Woodchip climb, shorter but punchier. Barriers also guarded the dirt incline to the finish line this year, so positioning was critical for the final half-mile effort. The new finish saw the women's field set up for a sprint as well.Johnson exploded from a reduced pack on the uphill charge to score the women's pro win by one second over 2023 champion Deanna Mayles. Making a first appearance at the 36-year-old mountain bike race, Johnson finished in 1:50:49. Erin Osbourne led a trailing trio for third place, her fifth consecutive top-five finish, with Crystal Anthony going fourth and Lily-Rose Marois fifth. From another group just a handful of seconds later, Samara Sheppard, Sierra Sims and Jenna Rinehart went sixth through eighth, respectively. "This year's course was a curveball for all those seasoned. A faster, shorter 'highway' on Vasa directly to Woodchip hill (no icebreaker) and a straight shot to the finish," Mayles wrote on Instagram."A group of nearly 15 women in the final miles into the last hills on the course. Not a whole lot of features to break up the big packs of pros sprinting into the finish."Though it wasn't "mountain bike-y" enough for the veterans, the Milligan University senior switched equipment and rode her gravel bike to seal the day. Johnson completed a season in the U23 field at the Life Time Grand Prix, finishing second to Kylee Hanel at Unbound Gravel 100 and went second in the U23 overall standings. After finishing 11th overall at Big Sugar Gravel, Johnson earned one of two MAAP Future of Off-Road Racing scholarships, which include cash and a spot on the 2027 MAAP PRO.FWD team in 2027. Olshove raced for the first time in the men's elite field at the Life Time Grand Prix this season, finishing outside the top 20. He performed well outside the series, taking top 10s at Belgian Waffle Ride Arizona and Rule of Three gravel races. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay
item.author: Barney Ronay
item.content:encoded: United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the leagueIn Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.Continue reading...

item.title: Inside a WorldTour pro's off-season: Watching NBA with Remco, much-needed days on the couch, and exhausting wind tunnel tests - Luke Tuckwell's column
item.author: Luke Tuckwell
item.content:encoded: If you've scrolled through social media over the past few weeks, you'd have come across countless posts from professional cyclists around the world enjoying their off-seasons and giving followers a small glimpse into what they have been doing. I'm guilty of this too. Posting 20 photos on Instagram of where I've been, what I’ve eaten, and who I’ve been spending my time with. It’s straight to the point. So today I'm going to give a deeper dive into what my off-season looked like, how it’s shaping my 2027 season, and why it was the best off-season I have had to date.I was one of the lucky pros at the end of this year (admittedly, that depends on how you define lucky) because I finished my season relatively early after a jam-packed neo pro season. The World Championships road race in Montreal was my final event of the 2026 season, and although I didn’t finish, I had a great time with the Australian team. It was a perfect way to close out the year. As I sat on the flight back to Barcelona, I had a strange feeling inside me, though. I didn’t really want the season to end. It had been so good to me, and I had enjoyed it so much. Being a neo pro was nice too. It gave me the luxury of making mistakes and not having as much pressure on my shoulders at races, and as you move further into your career, more is expected from you as an athlete.On the other hand, I was completely exhausted. I had 41 race days under my belt before July arrived without having raced the Giro, and rounded off the year by finishing my first Grand Tour at La Vuelta. I ended the season with 67 race days, almost the same as my 2024 and 2025 seasons combined. Needing time to do absolutely nothingI was well and truly ready to take some time for myself, sit on the couch for hours on end and enjoy the few weeks of the year when I can truly do whatever pleases me. After a few days at home post-travel back from Montreal, I planned to travel to the Basque Country in northern Spain with my parents and some family friends for a few days. But when the day came to travel, I was still completely exhausted, and all I wanted was to sit on the couch and spend some time in my own apartment. It was a good decision in the end, because after almost two weeks, when it was time for the ‘planned’ holiday part of my off-season, I already felt completely rested and my body was returning to normality, if that's how you want to call it. I wasn’t keen on any overseas holidays this year like a lot of my fellow pros do (I have these trips planned in my head for the coming years), but instead I wanted to stay local and avoid yet more air travel. Thankfully, the beautiful Costa Brava in northern Spain is only a three-and-a-half-hour drive from my home in Andorra. So I spent a wonderful, very relaxing few days there with my girlfriend, whose off-season it was too. We both recharged our batteries lying in the early autumn Spanish sun. By now, it had already been close to three weeks without the bike for me, and I was starting to get a bit antsy. Throughout this time, I tried to exercise to keep me sane, opting for walks or hikes. It felt nice to spend an hour outside every day just following a dirt track and seeing where it took me. I didn’t do any crazy hikes to mountain peaks like others do; I don’t have the required skill level for that. I stuck to what I knew because the last thing I wanted was to call up the team and tell them I can’t walk or start riding again because I'd sprained my ankle…By this point, the off-season finish line was edging closer and closer, but there were still two big requirements to tick off. First was my team’s annual October medical camp at Red Bull HQ in Austria, a jam-packed two days of tests at the Athlete Performance Centre (APC) followed by commercial shoots, all in preparation for the 2027 season. But the big ticket item of my off-season was still to come. Every year the team sends roughly six riders to Specialized HQ in Morgan Hill, California, for wind tunnel testing. I was fortunate enough to do this twelve months ago when I was still on the Rookies. But this year our trip had some extra flair. The realities of wind tunnel testingAlongside my teammates Remco Evenepoel and fellow Aussie Jai Hindley, I jetted off to the USA as part of the first group of riders, and this year we had a little side quest mission in Los Angeles to complete. After the twelve-hour flight from Munich to LA, we had a basketball game lined up that evening, the first NBA game I've watched in my life and a cool introduction to America’s sporting culture. We visited Red Bull’s APC in LA and toured their facilities across the pond. We played beach tennis, visited the Santa Monica Pier, took part in a community ride with Specialized Santa Monica, and carried out a cheeky recon of the potential LA 2028 Olympics ITT course. All in all, I haven’t laughed that much in a long time, and it truly felt like a Year 10 boys' school trip. But we still had the ‘work’ part of the trip to go: the wind tunnel testing at the Specialized WinTunnel.Without giving too much away, I personally made significant gains on my TT position thanks to all the new pieces of equipment developed by Specialized and the team. I am sure most of the readers of this are also aware of the wind tunnel testing Cyclingnews Labs carries out, but I want to give you an insight into how tough wind tunnel testing actually is on the body. For context, testing at Specialized is made up of six and a half-minute runs. So every time you change something, even the smallest detail, you complete one full run to gather data, and sometimes you even complete that same run twice to reinforce the findings. My time in the tunnel consisted of two morning sessions which ultimately ran into the early afternoon. On day one, I completed 18 runs, followed by a solid 24 runs the following day (I broke my personal 2025 record of 22 runs, so I was pleased). But the hardest part is consistently holding the extremely aggressive position on the time trial bike again and again and again. You get to the point where you cannot feel your arms anymore, and your back, neck, and shoulders are crying out for a moment of relief. But the pain is temporary; we are here to get faster, so you take down another can of Red Bull and keep going for another few hours.While you're in the tunnel with 50km/h wind blasting you in the face, all you can think about is how happy you will be once it’s all over, but to be honest, I look back on it with fond memories because it is such a rewarding experience. You can literally see how much faster you are getting with each run, and I can tell you that is a pretty special feeling knowing you are making those gains. I am already looking forward to the next time I get the opportunity to return to the WinTunnel.So that summarises my off-season. After a long journey back from Morgan Hill back to Andorra, I decided it wasn’t quite enough travelling for me, so I spent another twelve-hour day travelling to visit my girlfriend in Denmark. Yes, she is Danish, so don’t worry we didn’t just come to Denmark in early winter for fun. As I write this, I am ten days back into training and feeling extremely motivated for the new season. I'll spend another two weeks here in Denmark, two weeks back home in Andorra, two weeks in Mallorca for December camp, then travel back to Australia for Christmas and, all being well, I'll start my season at the Tour Down Under again. Thanks for taking the time to read this column. I hope you enjoyed it, and see you again soon.

item.title: 'If I start discussing contracts here, I think I'll go crazy' –Paul Seixas not thinking about future deal as off-season rolls on
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The future of French superstar Paul Seixas remains up in the air as the offseason rolls on, with the 20-year-old's Decathlon CMA CGM contract set to expire at the end of the 2027 season.Seixas is the brightest rising star in the sport, having won La Flèche Wallonne, Itzulia Basque Country, and Il Lombardia this season while finishing fourth in his debut Tour de France.Decathlon will be hoping to keep their leader on board well beyond then as he looks to challenge Tadej Pogačar and inherit the Slovenian's crown as the world's most dominant rider, though UAE Team Emirates-XRG are among the teams interested in his signature.Seixas is currently enjoying his off-season vacation in Asia, taking on the Tour de France Singapore Criterium before heading to its sister event in Saitama. He told that he's putting contract negotiations out of his mind for now, saying he'd "go crazy" if he devoted too much thinking time to the process."I'm on vacation right now. If I start discussing contracts here, I think I'll go crazy. I've taken this time to rest, and I figure if I don't think about it for now, things might be clearer when I think about it again. We'll see what I think about it in the future. But for now, I'm giving myself time," Seixas said."It’s a vacation, no doubt about it. I’m really enjoying it; I took the break I wanted. Of course, it makes for a busy day or two, but on the other hand, I’m enjoying being away and seeing things that are completely new to me, so it’s cool. The real restart will be on November 20th, a few days after Saitama, which gives me time to rest a bit and readjust. And then it’s back to racing."Despite not wanting to devote his mental space to thoughts of his future, Seixas acknowledged that it's a fact of life within the sport. He said that he finds speculation over his future as "pointless", however."I think it's part of the sport. It's normal that people talk about what's next; it's good, because it means that people are interested in me and want to know where I'm going," he said."Personally, though, I sometimes find it a bit pointless. Will I stay? Won't I stay? Right now, there's no certainty. Sometimes I come across articles, things on social media, and it makes me laugh a little because there are things I learn."Seixas did talk a little about his hopes for his future contract, wherever that may be. Rather than financial considerations occupying the forefront of his mind, he's instead prioritising other things."They could offer me the moon. It's a very difficult question for me," he said."I'm looking for a feeling, a connection. I want to really feel in sync with this team, with people I like. I think that's the most important thing, ultimately."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Relaxed Primož Roglič gets back on the bike for Taiwan Masters Ride despite time and options for finding new team in 2027 running low
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: While Primož Roglič's future in cycling remains one of the major unanswered questions ahead of the 2027 season, the Slovenian seems to be unfazed as he's headed to Asia for an appearance at the Taiwan Masters Ride.Five-time Grand Tour champion Roglic arrived in Taiwan last week as the headliner for the event, which saw him attempt to beat the KOM atop the Wuling Pass, around 200km south of Taipei. "I think it depends on the feeling or the state you are in, no? Normally it's just fatigue, so as you are tired and the body screams 'please stop', it's just a fight with that inner voice that wants to stop. You're sad, yes, but we'll just continue without hearing it," said Roglič in a promotional video for the Taiwan Masters Ride."The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you. I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."Roglič failed to beat the time, despite the help of Yen Yo Ho and Li Ting Wei, Taiwanese pro riders from Equipo Kern Pharma and Factor Racing, and four others. However, it had reportedly been weeks since the Slovenian had even ridden his bike amid his off-season holidays, and he didn't even bring his own bike with him, instead riding a grey S-Works Tarmac provided to him."What an incredible experience to have Primož Roglič take on one of Taiwan’s most beautiful and challenging cycling routes – the East-to-West Wuling Challenge! We also arranged six Taiwanese riders to take turns pacing him and helping him push toward the summit," read an Instagram post from Taiwanese TV anchor and cycling enthusiast Yu-Tien Wei, who also took part in the event."Unfortunately, he didn’t break the record this time. (Well, he hadn’t been on the bike for four whole weeks!) But seriously… is it even normal to ride like that after four weeks off the bike?!"Watching Roglič team up with the Taiwanese riders, taking turns at the front and giving everything they had to push up the mountain, was truly an incredible and inspiring moment. More than just a challenge, it was an unforgettable ride!"Roglič closed out the 2026 season at Il Lombardia after winning the European time trial title on home roads, having already finished second overall at the Vuelta a España behind Enric Mas in what was a remarkable recovery from being hit by a driver just a month before the start. He turned 37 in late October, but his results proved he is more than capable of still competing with the very best. With his departure from Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe confirmed earlier in the summer, the hunt for a new team began for Roglič, with Lotto-Intermarché, Pinarello Q36.5, Visma-Lease a Bike, Unibet Rose Rockets and Tudor among the teams rumoured as landing spots for Roglič in 2027. As the weeks have ticked by into November and closer to the January 1 start of the new racing season, all news surrounding Roglič so far has pointed to him potentially retiring. Just more than a week ago, reported that Lotto and Visma were both not going to happen, and reported on November 4 that Pinarello was looking unlikely. The speculation surrounding the other teams, too, had gone quiet, and there remains the question of whether Roglič actually wants to continue. In his typical style, he's been vague when answering questions about his future and his desires for a new team."It's beautiful, maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it," said Roglič, talking about the European Champion's jersey. "It would be hard to imagine a better end to the championship."Asked if he will continue to race next year, he said: "I don’t know it yet. We will see. We will see."But as for whether he wanted to, he replied: "I think so, yes. I think I will still race." Among active riders in the peloton, only his compatriot Tadej Pogačar has more professional victories than Roglič's 93, and as a four-time Vuelta winner, Giro d'Italia winner, and 22-time Grand Tour stage winner, he represents the old generation against the new wave of young stars, including the likes of Paul Seixas, Isaac del Toro, and Remco Evenepoel.When he returns home from Taiwan, Roglič should have decisions to make about whether he extends his time in the sport, and whether he can still find the drive and motivation to fight through setbacks and train to compete at the highest level. In 2026, he managed to show the grit he long has, since swapping ski jumping for pro cycling in 2014, but it could end up that his last ride as a professional was on a mountain in Taiwan, not the ideal send-off for one of the modern era's great champions. Perhaps an early trip into Slovenia on the recently announced Giro route can convince him to come back with a team where he gets the opportunity to properly bow out from the sport on his own terms, and he's also said openly that he wants to return to the Tour de France. The salary will likely be much lower than previous years if he does end up on a new team, but for the moment, retirement looks as likely a possibility as any.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Marianne Vos, Lotte Kopecky, Mathieu van der Poel, and Maddy Nutt among stars set to headline Rouleur Live in London
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: Newly crowned gravel World Champion Marianne Vos, Mathieu van der Poel, Lotte Kopecky and Maddy Nut are among the riders set to headline Rouleur Live in London this week, November 12-14. They will be appearing on stage alongside dozens of other pro cycling talents, including former Tour de France winner Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney.Vos is widely regarded as the greatest cyclist of all time and, throughout a multi-discipline career spanning 20 years, has won 15 elite world titles, most recently at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Australia, last month. The three-day event kicks off on Thursday November 12, with a line-up that includes multi-discipline World Champion and three-time winner of the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix, Van der Poel, along with Xaverine Nirere, Niewiadoma-Phinney and partner Taylor Phinney, who recently returned to track racing, and Bradley Wiggins.The event continues on Friday, November 13, with multi-time track and road World Champion Lotte Kopecky, former World Champion and this year's Tour de France green-jersey winner Mads Pedersen, Ben Healy, and Fabian Cancellara.The event will conclude on Saturday, November 14, with Vos taking the stage along with Matteo Trentin and gravel specialist Maddy Nutt.In between, figures from across the sport will attend the event, offering interviews and stage discussions throughout the three days. Rouleur Live, formerly known as The Rouleur Classic, began in 2015 in London and will be held this year at the Truman Brewery in East London.Cyclingnews will attend Rouleur Live on an invitation that includes complimentary admission on November 12 and 13. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser of the event or any sponsor.

item.title: Luxembourg federation lodges official complaint over Marie Schreiber's lost European title, but how can they hope to overturn the decision?
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Luxembourg's cycling federation has officially lodged a complaint in a bid to overturn and reinstate Marie Schreiber as the winner of the European Cyclo-cross title.Schreiber moved to the left in the two-up sprint to the line with Lucinda Brand (Netherlands), which the jury of UCI commissaires punished with relegation to second place, a decision that has proved controversial. "Following the women’s race at the European Cyclocross Championships, the FSCL officially filed a complaint with the UEC regarding the jury’s decision," read a statement."That is why the FSCL is calling for the race standings to be determined based on the order in which the riders crossed the finish line."How can the decision actually be appealed?It is unclear exactly how the FSCL hope to see the decision overturned.It states it has filed a complaint with the UEC, which organises the European Championships but does not officiate them from a disciplinary point of view. This responsibility, as with all UCI-sanctioned races, falls to the UCI, which applies its rulebook via a jury made up of a number of commissaires. The UCI's regulations state that infringements relating to race incidents – of which an irregular sprint is one – "are not subject to appeal", except for any fine that has been applied. So the monetary element of a punishment can be disputed but nothing else. However, the UCI's regulations do leave some wiggle room, later stating that its Disciplinary Commission, which usually deals with more general and more serious issues, can intervene and even overturn a decision."The Disciplinary Commission may, at its own initiative or upon request, decide to suspend the implementation of a decision by the Commissaires' Panel," state the UCI regulations. The Disciplinary Commission can decide on race infringements "which may have an influence on the sporting conduct or the result of an event", such as this one. However, the same section of the rulebook also states that the Disciplinary Commission can step in "in case the facts were not observed by the Commissaires' Panel or in case all relevant facts for the assessment of the infringement were not available at the time the Commissaires’ Panel disbanded". Only in the latter case will the decision of the Disciplinary Commission replace that of the Commissaires' Panel, according to the rules. What this suggests is that the Disciplinary Commission steps in when there's been a flaw in the process – not to review a fully-informed judgement made by a commissaire. In this case, the commissaires had all the facts available in the form of the video footage, so it's difficult to see any provision for overturning their decision under this section of the rulebook. Schreiber and the Luxembourg federation could in theory take legal action and lodge a case with the international Court of Arbitration for Sport, where the UCI is regularly challenged on disciplinary decisions. item.title: How the Racing Bulls pendulum is swinging back towards Lawson
'Give Mathieu those five seconds, and you won’t see him again' – Thibau Nys chasing Van der Poel's level of cyclo-cross dominance
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: After scoring his second career European Cyclo-cross Championships title in Zeddam on Sunday, Thibau Nys has said that he aspires to reach the level of Mathieu van der Poel in terms of of not just winning races but dominating them. The 23-year-old Belgian soloed to glory after leaving behind Joran Wyseure on the final lap of the race, adding the 2026 title to his triumph two years ago.Nys won five 'cross races last year, including three rounds of the UCI World Cup en route to second place overall in the series – behind Mathieu van der Poel. Now, he's set his sights on being able to convert his strength into the sort of victories Van der Poel has pulled off year after year."Just now on the podium, one side of me was happy with what I had already achieved, while the other side was already thinking about what could be better," Nys told after the victory, his second in two starts this season after opening his account with glory in the opening round of the X2O Trofee Koppenbergcross in Oudenaarde."Where can I find those extra percentages? Why can’t I just keep riding alone from lap four? In that fourth lap, for example, I unexpectedly gained a small gap, but I immediately felt that I didn’t have the legs to ride at the front by myself for the rest of the race."Give Mathieu (van der Poel) those five seconds, and you won’t see him again for the entire race. That is what I want to get to too, although I don’t know if I will ever be able to."Nys and his Belgian teammate Wyseure were neck-and-neck for much of the race, with Nys unable to go clear at the front before his final-lap effort. In the end, it wasn't a performance reminiscent of Van der Poel's dominant best, but Nys knows what he's aiming for."I felt I was really good, but not good enough to just ride ahead on my own for six or seven laps. So it was a bit of a feeling-out process and trying to see where I could create a gap, to then really explode on the last lap," he told ."Joran was riding at a very high pace and was simply able to maintain a strong tempo. In that respect, he was perhaps slightly stronger than me, but I did have that burst of energy a bit more in the final lap."We are really talking about details here, but I did feel, especially in the penultimate lap, that I perhaps had just a little more in reserve on those stairs to strike there in the final lap. And in the end, I managed to do just that."Nys has put a challenging road racing season blighted by knee surgery behind him to get off to a 100% start on the 'cross bike. Sterner tests lie ahead, including the World Championships at the end of January, as well as battles against Wout van Aert and possibly Van der Poel, who has yet to confirm his cyclo-cross plans for the winter. Fastest lap is not enough to overcome a slow start for Cameron Mason sixth at UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships
item.author: Lyne Lamoureux
item.content:encoded: A slow start derailed Cameron Mason’s quest to step back onto the podium in the elite men’s race at the UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships on Sunday. Starting on the second row, the British champion was in 27th place after Swiss rider Kevin Kuhn, who also started on the second row, took the holeshot and led the field onto the tough course in Zeddam, in the Netherlands.One lap later, as the field was stretching out and gaps started to form, Mason was 17 seconds back, in 23rd position. Not giving up, the 26-year-old started to give chase, trying to pick his way through the riders on a technical course which offered limited spots to pass.At the start of the sixth of nine laps, Mason had moved up to 10th place, at 21 seconds back. But at that point, three riders, including eventual winner Thibau Nys (Belgium), had pulled away.After putting a massive turn of speed on lap seven, Mason set the fastest lap of the race in 6:19, one second quicker than Nys. He then bridged across to a three-rider chase group, which was rapidly closing the gap and caught Kuhn on the penultimate lap.With only two riders up front, the bronze medal was still at play. So Mason went to the front of the chase group, coming as close as seven seconds to the leading duo, but the other riders in the group could not or would not provide assistance, and the gap grew out.By the start of the bell lap, the chase group was at 12 seconds and locked in battle for third place, which was ultimately taken by Niels Vandeputte (Belgian). Crossing the line in sixth place, Mason is still looking to equal or beat his second place in 2023 in Pontchâteau, France.“I didn’t stop believing until one lap to go, when I threw it all away. Even after the shocking position I put myself in on the first part of the race, I wasn’t raised to be a quitter,” Mason wrote on social media. “Today, like with the rest of life, I realised no one is going to do it for you. There will be many wonderful people who will help, guide and believe in you. But when it really matters, it’s all on you.”“That’s why today hurts so much. To show just how much I wanted it, but to fall short of a result on paper. “But what a privilege it is to put my heart and soul into doing hard things. I will be back.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: ‘Why not?’ - Isaac Del Toro on a Mexican rider winning Tour de France in the future
item.author: Lyne Lamoureux
item.content:encoded: Competing at the top level for the past two years, since his breakthrough at the 2024 Tour Down Under, Isaac del Toro has done more than win. He has also learned from both his successes and mistakes, something that he repeats in interviews, as he did on the eve of the Singapore Criterium.The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider enjoyed a remarkable 2026 season which included winning the overall at four WorldTour stage races: the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico, the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and the Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal. He also won a stage and finished third overall on his Tour de France debut, helping team leader Tadej Pogačar secure his fifth overall victory.Speaking on media day ahead of the Singapore exhibition race, which he went on to win, Del Toro told he was “very happy” with his season.“Happy to have had all the experiences this year and satisfied because I know I can apply them to the future to always do a little better. Obviously, with that emphasis on continuing to work hard.”From racing his first WorldTour race in Australia for UAE Emirates XRG at just 20 years of age, Del Toro quickly matured into taking on the mantle of team leader two years later.“It's something we tried to achieve from the moment I signed. We didn't know how quickly or slowly it would happen, or if it was even possible in such a competitive team where everyone is at a very high level,” Del Toro said.His progression began at the Tour Down Under, but Del Toro initially preferred to delay taking on leadership responsibilities as long as possible so he could learn from those around him.“After a year, I developed more and began to understand what kind of rider I am; I can handle myself well in quite a few situations, although I don't know if I specialise in anything.”As only the second Mexican rider to win a Tour de France stage, following Raúl Alcalá's victories in 1989 and 1990, Del Toro understands the responsibility that he carries, though he admits to sometimes forgetting it “for a moment”.“They remind you that you're a public figure, and you try to be measured. I know there's someone expecting something from me and trying to put me in the best possible light, so I take that as a responsibility.”When asked if it could be possible for a Mexican rider to win the Tour de France in the future, Del Toro replied: “Why not?”It wasn’t that long ago that the idea of having a Slovenian dominate racing would have raised eyebrows.“If others have won it, why can't a Mexican? We have two legs, two arms, a head... I don't see it as distant or impossible. It's difficult, but I see the same possibilities as everyone else.”“I won my first stage in Barcelona, I made the podium in the Giro, and I know I can be competitive. More athletes are coming up over the years; I'm not just referring to myself, but to the fact that, as Mexicans, of course it's possible.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. 'The most ridiculous reaction I have ever heard' – Three-time world champion Sanne Cant blasts UCI jury over Marie Schreiber’s relegation
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: After crossing the line first in the elite women’s race on Saturday, Schreiber was relegated to second place for an irregular sprint, the Luxembourg rider missing out on what would have been the biggest result of her career. It was clear from the head-on coverage that she did make a move to her left, but despite eventual winner Lucinda Brand asserting she was not impeded, the race jury interpreted this as a breach serious enough to warrant the relegation.Not only was Schreiber upset by the issue, but she has been joined by Cant, who has been part of the SD Worx team for two winters, and previously won three rainbow jerseys among 126 race wins during a long career. "It is the most ridiculous reaction I have ever heard," Cant told after the race. "I spent a very long time on a bike myself and I have never experienced anything like this. If we already find a mistake here... I think there are other sprints taking place on the road where nothing happens."Brand did not file a complaint, according to her Dutch cycling federation. "It really was the UCI president [of the commissaire's panel] who saw it, but it is anyone's guess what he saw," Cant said. "Maybe he should try sprinting on a 'cross bike himself. It will never be straight. I think the track was wide enough to pass."Schreiber did not attend the podium ceremony, which, according to reports in the Belgian press, was a decision that came primarily from Cant. "I didn't want her to stand on [the podium]. That is not because there is no respect for Lucinda, but because you shouldn't accept a medal that doesn't belong to you," Cant told . Cant added that "we are not going to leave it at this", and while it is unclear what action SD Worx-Protime might be able to take, given that the European Championships are contested by national teams, the Luxembourg cycling federation has announced it will appeal the decision.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: European Cyclo-cross Championships: Thibau Nys wins second elite title as Belgium sweeps the podium
item.author: Lyne Lamoureux
item.content:encoded: Thibau Nys powered away from his Belgian compatriot Joran Wyseure on the final lap on the slippery, heavy course to win his second elite men’s title at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam, Netherlands on Sunday. Wyseure crossed the line seven seconds later to claim silver, bettering his third place from last year. Completing an all-Belgian podium. Niels Vandeputte took bronze, winning the sprint from a four-rider chase group.With the largest squads in the race, Belgium fielding eight riders and the Netherlands five, the two teams took turns in the early laps, forcing the other to expend energy closing gaps on the slippery, heavy course. The tactical battle between the eternal rivals continued until Nys launched an attack on an off-camber section leading into the long stairs. Kuhn responded immediately, with Wyseure on his wheel.Nys and Wyseure pulled away with three laps to go, and battled each other until Nys put in a big acceleration, opening up a gap on the stairs and holding it to the finish line. “A tough one. I think it was a hard and a really nice battle with Joran. He was super strong and it was really difficult to get rid of each other, so I felt halfway through the race that it will be a big explosion in the last lap," Nys said.Nys agreed that the course was demanding: “It is, I mean, it is quite hard, but on the other hand, it's quite difficult to make a gap. And especially when you have to pull in the front on the section on the road on the finish line, it takes away a lot of energy, and it was a bit of a gamble over there.”“There is a lot more to come. For me, every race is just as important as another one, and next week is just as important as today’s the European Championships. So yeah, I will try to let the jersey shine.”Zeddam already hosted the 2006 Cyclocross World Championships, won by Erwin Vervecken (Belgium) and Marianne Vos (Netherlands). 34 riders, staged across five rows, took on the updated 2.97 km course, designed by the same Vervecken. The toughest obstacle was the revamped staircase with its 99 steps, used for the first time in a championship course. Also new was a 60-meter-long rider bridge alongside the Grafelijke Korenmolen, the oldest still-operating windmill in the Netherlands.Kevin Kuhn (Switzerland) took the holeshot, surging from the second row on the long, slightly uphill start straight, and led the pack on the first lap. Spain’s Felipe Orts took over setting the pace on the second lap, while Cameron Mason (Great Britain), after a slow start, was 22 seconds back.The tactical battle ended when Belgian Thibau Nys launched an attack on an off-camber section leading into the stairs. Kuhn responded immediately, with Belgian Joran Wyseure on his wheel, getting a free ride.By the start of the fourth lap, Nys had four seconds on Kuhn and Wyseure, and then 14 seconds on the second chase group, which organised behind Ryan Kamp (Netherlands). Once a gap was established to the group behind, Wyseure came to the front and reeled in his compatriot. Behind, Joris Nieuwenhuis (Netherlands), with Belgian duo Michael Vanthourenhout and Niels Vandeputte close by, launched from the chase group.Nys continued to apply pressure, as Kuhn fell off the pace, while Wyseure worked hard to get back on by the start of the seventh lap. Kuhn, 10 seconds back, was caught on the stairs by Orts, Vandeputte, Nieuwenhuis and Mason, leading to a five-way battle for the bronze medal.Coming into the ninth and final lap, Nys ooked behind him across the 12-second gap at the chasing group, before putting a big acceleration to drop Wyseure. He built on a slight gap opened on the stairs, to power on to take the win. Michael Vanthourenhout (Bel)Kevin Andre Sandli Messel (Nor)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Singapore Criterium: Isaac Del Toro takes surprise solo win as the sprinters miss out
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Isaac del Toro continued his battle with rival Paul Seixas on Sunday, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider taking a surprise solo win in the Singapore Criterium.Both he and Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) had been part of a four-man group which escaped the bunch on the 23rd lap around the city. As the final lap approached, the Mexican champion simply rode off the front of that group, holding Seixas a few seconds behind him until the line.Seixas hung on for second place, a handful of seconds behind, with Søren Warenskjold (UNO X Mobility) winning the sprint for third place. The peloton crossed the line some 30 seconds behind.With the traditional Saitama Criterium in Japan coming next weekend, Singapore was the first of two Far Eastern criteriums arranged by the Tour de France organisers, ASO, with the race taking place over 25 laps of a two-kilometre city circuit. The race started aggressively and remained that way throughout, with multiple breakaways going clear all day long. The first of those got away after the opening intermediate sprint and contained Baptiste Viestroffer (Lotto-Intermarché), Patrick Konrad (Lidl-Trek), home road champion Eamon Lim (CCACHE-BODYWRAP) and Rasmus Søjberg Pedersen (Decathlon-CMA CGM). They were away for a handful of laps, but the intermediate sprints, which came every five laps, dictated the race, the peloton re-forming before each one.That meant that none of the breakaways, however large, were able to gain any kind of advantage, with 10 seconds being all most would create. Biniam Girmay won the first intermediate sprint, and his NSN team were instrumental in containing the breakaways’ ambitions. Even a strong group of six was unable to build a lead as the race approached the final kick, with five laps of the race to go.One lap after that final sprint, French sensation Seixas let an all-star group of four up the road, with Del Toro, Mauro Schmid (Jayco-AlUla) and Søren Waerenskjold (UNO X Mobility) quickly establishing a lead and taking 10 seconds into the final three laps. With little conviction in the chase, their lead expanded and, at the start of the penultimate lap, that advantage was out to 30 seconds, the greatest advantage of any of the day’s breaks, and the race seemed set to end with a four-up sprint.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. 'It’s disrespectful to steal the biggest moment of my career' - Marie Schreiber condemns Euro cyclo-cross relegation
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Schreiber crossed the line first in the Elite Women’s race at Zeddam in the Netherlands, apparently bagging the biggest win of her career, but a few minutes later, she was relegated for an irregular sprint. She later refused to attend the podium ceremony."The UCI and UEC they always advocate for and everyone they always advocate for clean and fair sport and then they do this, it’s unfair," Schreiber said after the race.She and World Champion Lucinda Brand (Netherlands) had come into the finish straight together after the Luxembourgish rider overtook on the brutal run up the flight of 99 steps. Leading out, Schreiber opened her sprint early, holding Brand at bay. From the footage, it was clear she did move to her left as the pair closed in on the finish line, and it seems it was this move the race commissaires penalised."We reviewed the footage and both me and Lucinda said our views," Schreiber said. "Lucinda said I did nothing wrong, she couldn’t have passed anyway, so I think it’s really thankful that she said this, but it doesn’t change the commissaires’ decision. "It’s a sprint after 50 minutes of all out racing, you come with 190 heart rate, I change my gear, I saw I moved a little bit to the left, but then I think if every person watches the race you know this moving around it’s normal. I did not close the door on purpose or anything, Lucinda knows this and she also said it. "I think it’s disrespectful to steal the biggest moment of my career just for this because I think for being fair everyone knows I won, if it would have been decided by two centimetres I can argue with them I can understand, but like this I think it’s just disrespectful to be honest."Though Schreiber was relegated to second place, with Brand’s compatriot Ceylon del Carmen Alvarado in third, she was not present on the podium, and was asked if her team manager, former World Champion Sanne Can’t, had advised her not to attend, something which may mean she is fined by the race jury."Yeah, I was going to go because I thought everyone’s going to hate me if I don’t go, but then it’s like if they’re being like this to me then I also don’t owe them anything, to be honest. It’s hard to be standing here right now, so you can imagine it’s harder to stand on the podium, so they said I shouldn’t go, I shouldn’t let myself be treated like this. I can live with a fine probably better than going to sleep tonight."Though she has a World Cup race win to her name, victory in the Euros would have been by far the biggest success of Schreiber’s career. Riding for her road trade team, SD Worx-Protime, Schreiber has had an excellent start to the 2026/27 season, winning the two opening races of the year, taking three more wins, with third place at the X2O Koppenbergcross her worst result.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’
item.author: Niha Masih
item.content:encoded: A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artisticprocess and personal relationships in hisfinal yearsIt’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.Continue reading...

item.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying
item.author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
item.content:encoded: Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal importsBritish government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.Continue reading...
